passages.title: The Originator, His angels, and the mercy none can withhold
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 1 praises Allah and names two grounds for that praise: He is *Fatir* — the Originator — of the heavens and the earth, and He is the One who made the angels messengers. Ayah 2 states that whatever mercy Allah opens for people, no one can hold it back, and whatever He withholds, no one else can release. Ayah 3 turns to all mankind and asks whether there is any creator besides Allah who provides from the sky and the earth.

Ibn Kathir, commenting on ayah 3, gives the reasoning that ties the passage together: Allah shows His servants that they should worship Him alone, **for just as He is Independent in His power of creation and provision, so He should be worshipped alone**, with no partners or associates such as idols and false gods. Reading the three ayat in the light of that sentence — and this joining-up is my own way of holding them together, not a claim made in the commentaries — the movement runs: He originates, He assigns even the messengers, He alone opens and withholds, and therefore He alone is worthy of worship.

## "All praise is for Allah, Fatir of the heavens and the earth"

The surah begins with *al-hamdu lillah*, all praise is due to Allah, and immediately names the reason for it: *Fatir as-samawati wal-ard*.

There is a lovely report in Ibn Kathir about how this word was understood. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I did not know what *Fatir As-Samawati wal-Ard* meant until two bedouins came to me disputing over a well. One of them said to his companion, *'Ana Fatartuha'*" — meaning, "**I started it**."

That everyday usage is the flavour of *fatir*: the one who *starts* the thing. Ibn 'Abbas himself glossed the phrase as "the Originator of the heavens and the earth," and Ad-Dahhak said that every time the phrase *Fatir As-Samawati wal-Ard* is used in the Qur'an, it means the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

Notice what that does to the praise. The heavens and the earth, in all their scale, are not being admired for their own sake; they are traced back to the One who originated them. Ibn Kathir gathers this whole ayah under a single heading: **The Power of Allah.**

## The angels: messengers with wings

*Ja'il al-mala'ikati rusula* — "Who made the angels messengers."

Messengers between whom and whom? Ibn Kathir answers plainly: **between Him and His Prophets.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point at more length — the angels were assigned to convey the messages and injunctions of Allah, and from this it is obvious that they are sent to the noble prophets as the message-bearers or envoys of Allah, conveying His revelations and injunctions to them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then offers a second possibility for the word *rasul* here: it may be denoting the sense of a **link**. On that reading, the angels become a link between Allah and His universal creation, of which the noble prophets are the superior-most — so their part in transmitting revelation is one instance of that wider office. These same angels, it adds, happen to be the means of bringing the mercy of Allah, or His punishment, to the creation.

Either way, the word to sit with is *ja'il*: He *made* them messengers. They were assigned. That is what makes their mention fitting in an ayah of praise.

**"Having wings, in twos and threes and fours."** Ibn Kathir explains the wings as those "with which they fly to convey quickly that which they have been commanded to convey." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the wise consideration behind it: Allah has given the angels feathered wings they can fly with, because they traverse the distance between the heavens and the earth repeatedly, and that is possible only with the necessary speed to do so — something that comes about in the mode of flying alone.

So the wings are told to us as a detail of function: the sheer *speed* at which the command of Allah is carried.

**Are the numbers a limit?** Both commentaries say no. Ibn Kathir: among them are some who have two wings, some three, some four — and some have more than that, as stated in the Hadith mentioning that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw Jibril, peace be upon him, on the Night of the Isra' with six hundred wings, the distance between each pair of wings being like that between the east and the west. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about the numbers being given as an example rather than an inventory, and notes that Jibril's six hundred is proved by a Hadith in the *Sahih* of Muslim, citing Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a second grammatical possibility, from Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr ul-Muhit*. The three words "twos and threes and fours" may be numerical adjectives referring not to *ajnihah* (wings) but to *rusulan* (the bearers of the message) — meaning that the angels who deliver messages from Allah to this world sometimes come in twos, at others in threes or fours. Here too, Abu Hayyan notes, four is not intended as a restriction but as an example, since the coming of angels in a much larger number stands proved from the Qur'an itself.

The commentaries set these two parsings side by side; I have reported them as they stand.

## "He increases in creation what He wills"

*Yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha'.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the sentence as meaning that Allah has the power to increase whatever He wills, and as much as He wills, in the creation of everything He has originated.

**The first reading — most commentators.** This is related to the wings just mentioned: the feathers and wings of the angels are not restricted to two or four, for they could be many more than these if Allah so wills. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most commentators say exactly this. As-Suddi, cited by Ibn Kathir, said: "He increases their wings and creates them as He wills."

**The second reading — general.** The tafsir authorities Zuhri, Qatadah and others held that this increase in creation is to be taken in its general sense, which includes the increase in the feathers and wings of angels as well as the increase of particular attributes in the creation of different human beings — the beauty of form, the beauty of character, the beauty of voice, and many more increased assets like these. Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr ul-Muhit*, followed this same track and said that things like good manners, beauty of figure and face, perfection of reason and intellect, politeness in discourse and similar others are all included in it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion from this second reading, and it is worth sitting with: **this second tafsir proves that the beauty or perfection of anything one has is invariably a gift and blessing from Allah, for which one should be grateful to Him.** Take the qualities the commentators actually name — a person's form and face, character and manners, voice, soundness of reason, courtesy in speech. Not one of them is an achievement you brought to the table. Each is an increase Allah placed in you as He willed, and gratitude is owed for it.

The ayah then seals it: **"Verily, Allah is Able to do all things."**

## Ayah 2: the two doors

> "Whatever of mercy Allah may grant to mankind, none can withhold it; and whatever He may withhold, none can grant it thereafter. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise."

Ibn Kathir places this under the heading **None can withhold the Mercy of Allah**, and states the meaning in one line: Allah tells us that what He wills happens, and what He does not will does not happen. **None can give what He withholds, and none can withhold what He gives.**

**How wide is "mercy" here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the word *rahmah* is general in this place. It includes the blessings of one's religion in this world along with those of the Hereafter — faith, knowledge, rightly guided conduct, as well as the mission of a prophet and the station of a *Waliyy*, a man of Allah. And it includes material blessings in the present world — provisions, means, comfort, health, wealth, property, recognition and things like that. The ayah is not narrowly about rain, or money, or guidance. It reaches every good thing there is.

The Arabic verb is *yaftah*, to **open**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the sense plainly: the person for whom Allah intends to open the doors of His mercy — there is no one who can stop it.

**And the second half is just as general.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Abu Hayyan, notes that *wa ma yumsik*, "whatever He holds back," is likewise general: what Allah holds back cannot be released by anyone. This includes the hardships and sorrows of the world — when Allah intends to shield some servant of His from these, there is no one who can dare harass or harm him. And it includes the matter of mercy as well: should Allah decide to deprive a person of His mercy due to some wise consideration of His, there is no one who can dare pass it on to him.

That last phrase is worth noticing, because the ayah closes with **al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm**, the Almighty, the All-Wise. Abu Hayyan's wording ties the withholding to "some wise consideration of His" — power that is absolute, and never without wisdom.

Ibn Kathir places alongside this ayah its close parallel: "And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none who can remove it but He; and if He intends any good for you, there is none who can repel His favour" (10:107) — and notes that there are many similar ayat.

## From the Sunnah: the words the Prophet ﷺ said after prayer

The meaning of this ayah has a striking footprint in the Sunnah.

**After the salah.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Warrad, the freed slave of Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah: Mu'awiyah wrote to Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah saying, "Write for me what you heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." So Al-Mughirah called Warrad, and he wrote: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say when he finished praying:

> *La ilaha illa Allah, wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu'l-mulku wa lahu'l-hamd, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir. Allahumma la mani'a lima a'tayta, wa la mu'tiya lima mana'ta, wa la yanfa'u dha'l-jaddi minka'l-jadd*
>
> "There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, with no partner or associate. To Him be praise and dominion, and He is able to do all things. O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold, and good fortune and richness in anything cannot benefit one against Your will."

Warrad's letter continued: he also heard him forbid gossiping, asking too many questions and wasting money, burying girls alive, disobeying one's mother, and withholding from others while asking from them. Ibn Kathir notes that this was also recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim, with several chains of narration. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the same report, citing Ibn Kathir from the *Musnad* of Ahmad.

Look at the structure of that dhikr and you will see ayah 1 and ayah 2 standing next to each other: *"He is able to do all things"* closes ayah 1; *"none can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold"* is the substance of ayah 2. The believer says the meaning of this passage back to Allah at the end of the prayer.

**After rising from ruku'.** Ibn Kathir records that it was reported in Sahih Muslim that Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his head from bowing, he would say: 'Allah hears those who praise Him. O Allah, our Lord, to You be praise, filling the heavens and the earth, and filling whatever You wish besides. O Allah, the One deserving praise and glory. The truest words that any servant says — and all of us are Your servants — are: O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold, and no wealth or majesty can benefit anyone against Your will.'"

Pause on that phrase: **"the truest words that any servant says."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same clause as meaning that these words, out of all that a servant of Allah can say, are the most true, incumbent and superior.

A note on the closing wording: Muhammad Taqi Usmani observes that the translation above rests on one way of reading it — as *jidd*, with a kasrah on the letter *jim*, giving the sense that no efforts by any maker of effort work against Your will. But if it is read as *jadd*, the correct translation would be that no high status of a person may benefit him against Your decree.

## Living it: where to point your hope and your fear

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *Ruh ul-Ma'ani*, states the lesson this ayah teaches all human beings: **one should not hope any benefit or fear any harm from anyone other than Allah; instead, one should keep his or her sight trained towards Allah alone.** It calls this the master prescription for a better life in this world as well as the life to come — a simple antidote that delivers one from thousands of anxieties and sorrows.

Read that against how worry actually works, and the description earns its name. Much of our anxiety comes from treating created things as the real sources of good and harm — a manager, a market, a diagnosis, a rival. The ayah does not say those things are unreal; it says they are not the ones who open and withhold.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two illustrations that make this concrete.

**'Amir Ibn 'Abd Qays** said: once I get to recite four verses of the noble Qur'an in the morning, I stop worrying about what would happen in the morning and what would happen in the evening. They are (1) this very ayah, 35:2; (2) "And if Allah causes you some harm, no one is there to remove it except He Himself; and if He causes you some good, then He is powerful over everything" (6:17); (3) "Allah will soon bring ease after a difficulty" (65:7); and (4) "And there is no creature on earth whose sustenance is not on Allah" (11:6). This is narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir, as in *Ruh ul-Ma'ani*.

Four ayat, recited at the start of the day — a worked example of turning this passage into a habit.

**Abu Hurairah and the rain.** When Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, saw rain falling, he used to say *"Mutirna bi-naw' al-fath"* — "the rain has come upon us through the rise of *fath*, the opening" — and would then recite *"Whatever blessing Allah opens for the people, there is none to hold it back."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that his term "rise of *fath*" was in rebuttal of a false notion prevailing among the Arabs of those days, who attributed the coming of rains to the rise of particular stars and would say the rain had come upon them through the rise of such-and-such star. Abu Hurairah countered it by saying that the rain came to him through the verse of *fath*, of opening, and he used to recite it particularly on such occasions. This is reported by Imam Malik in *al-Muwatta*.

It is a small, deliberate act of speech, and a usable model. Where a culture credits a mechanism, luck, or a cycle, the believer names the One who opened the channel — without denying that the rain fell.

## Ayah 3: the argument closes

> "O mankind! Remember the grace of Allah upon you! Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you from the sky and the earth? *La ilaha illa Huwa.* How then are you turning away?"

The address widens to **all mankind**, and the first command is *remember*. What is offered as evidence is provision that is already in your hands: rain from the sky — Ibn Kathir glosses "from the sky" as rain — and provision from the earth.

Ibn Kathir titles this section **The Evidence of Tawhid** and states the logic exactly: Allah shows His servants that they should worship Him alone, for **just as He is Independent in His power of creation and provision, so He should be worshipped alone**, with no partners or associates such as idols and false gods.

That is the argument of the passage in a sentence, and the earlier ayat feed it. Ayah 1: He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and even the angels who carry His messages were *made* such by Him. Ayah 2: no mercy He opens can be held back, and nothing He holds back can be released by anyone else. Therefore ayah 3: there is no second creator and no second provider — so there is no second object of worship. *La ilaha illa Huwa.*

And so the closing question, *fa-anna tu'fakun*, "how then are you turning away?" Ibn Kathir renders its force as: how can you turn away from Him after this has been made clear and this proof has been made obvious, and still worship idols and false gods? And Allah knows best.

The question is not decoration. After a case laid out this plainly, turning away is not a shortage of information. The passage leaves the reader nowhere else to stand — which is why it opened, and deserves to close, with *al-hamdu lillah*.

passages.title: Comfort for the rejected Prophet; Satan's deception
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat turn from the majesty of Allah described in the surah's opening to the rejection the Messenger ﷺ was facing: he is being called a liar by those who associate others with Allah. Allah steadies him, and then widens the address to all of humanity, warning against two deceptions — the glitter of this present life, and the whisper of an enemy who has already declared his hostility.

What holds the passage together is a single chain of thought: *they deny you, but everything returns to Allah for judgement (4) — and that judgement is real, so do not be fooled about it, whether by the world or by the chief deceiver (5) — that deceiver is your declared enemy, and his invitation ends in the Fire (6) — hence two destinies, punishment and forgiveness (7) — and hence a man can be so far gone that his own evil looks beautiful to him, at which point your grief cannot save him, so do not let it destroy you (8).* It opens with comfort for the Prophet ﷺ and closes with comfort for the Prophet ﷺ, and everything in between explains why the rejection happened.

## Ayah 4: "So too were messengers before you"

Ibn Kathir renders the sense of ayah 4 as Allah saying: *even if these idolaters who associate others with Allah disbelieve in you, O Muhammad, and go against the message of Tawhid that you have brought, you have an example in the Messengers who came before you.* They too brought a clear message to their people; they too told them to worship Allah alone; and their people denied them and went against them.

Notice how the consolation works. Allah does not tell His Prophet ﷺ that the pain is small. He reframes the rejection: this is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the mission — it is the standing experience of the men Allah sent. Being disbelieved is what happened to prophets. The one who is denied is in the noblest company there is.

Then the second half: **وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ ٱلْأُمُورُ** — "and to Allah return all matters." Ibn Kathir gives its force in a few words: "We will requite them for that in full." The matter is not dropped; it is filed. Nothing said against the Messenger ﷺ is lost, and no one who said it has escaped. A believer who is mocked for his religion is being handed exactly this consolation: you are not required to settle the account, because the account is not yours, and it is not closed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same lesson from the surah's earlier ayah about Allah's mercy (35:2) — that a servant should neither hope for benefit nor fear harm from anyone other than Allah, but keep his sight trained towards Allah alone. It calls this the master prescription for a better life in this world as well as in the life to come, a simple antidote that delivers a person from thousands of anxieties and sorrows (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī). That is precisely the medicine ayah 4 hands to a rejected Prophet ﷺ: the opinion of the deniers changes nothing, because they hold nothing in their hands.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records in this connection a report that Muʿāwiyah (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah (may Allah be pleased with him), his governor at Kufah, asking him to send back in writing some hadith he had personally heard from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Mughīrah called his chief scribe and dictated that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ, soon after finishing his salah, reciting: *"O Allah, for what You give there is none to stop it, and for what You hold back there is none to give it out, and no efforts by any maker of effort work against Your will."* Maʿārif cites this from Ibn Kathir, from the *Musnad* of Ahmad. It also notes a narration of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him) in the *Sahih* of Muslim, in which these words were said on raising the head from rukūʿ, along with the statement that these words, out of all that a servant of Allah can say, are the most true, incumbent and superior.

Take those words onto your own tongue after prayer and ayah 4 has entered your bloodstream: what people give or withhold from you — respect, acceptance, a hearing — was never theirs to give.

## Ayah 5: two deceptions, one target

Having consoled His Messenger ﷺ, Allah widens the address: **يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ** — "O humanity."

"Indeed Allah's promise is true." Ibn Kathir: this means the Resurrection will undoubtedly come to pass. That is the hinge of the whole passage. Before any argument is made, the Day of Judgement is put back at the centre — and the two warnings that follow are both about being *fooled*, the same prohibition twice over:

**فَلَا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ ٱلْحَيَاةُ ٱلدُّنْيَا** — "so let not this present life deceive you." Ibn Kathir explains: this life is as nothing in comparison to the great good that Allah has promised to His close friends and the followers of His Messengers, so do not let these transient attractions distract you from that which is lasting. The world's deception is not that it lies about being pleasant. It is that it presents itself as the whole picture, when it is a fragment.

**وَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكُم بِٱللَّهِ ٱلْغَرُورُ** — "and let not the chief deceiver deceive you about Allah." Who is *al-gharūr*? Ibn Kathir reports that this refers to Shaytan, as stated by Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him): do not let Shaytan tempt you and divert you away from following the Messengers of Allah and believing what they say, for he is the chief deceiver and arch-liar.

**A note on the word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *gharūr* is an emphatic form of an adjective meaning "one who is very deceiving" — hence "big deceiver." Maʿārif puts his role starkly: his sole job is to deceive people and throw them into disbelief and sin.

**Deceived *about Allah*.** The phrase is precise: not merely "deceived," but deceived *concerning Allah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it on the authority of Qurṭubī: Shaytan's technique is to show your evil deeds as good, causing you to become so involved with them that you reach the stage where you go on committing a sin while at the same time keeping the thought that you are of those accepted in the sight of Allah, and that you will not have to undergo any punishment. This is the most dangerous outcome possible, because it disables the very faculty that would fix it. A man who knows he is sinning may repent. A man who believes his sin is virtue has nothing to repent from.

Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah is like the ayah at the end of Surah Luqman (31:33) — the same double warning about this present life and the chief deceiver, in almost the same words.

## Ayah 6: "So take him as an enemy"

**إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَـٰنَ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّ فَٱتَّخِذُوهُ عَدُوًّا** — "Surely Shaytan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy."

Read the two halves carefully. The first is a statement of fact; the second is a command about your posture. Ibn Kathir catches it exactly: *he has declared his enmity towards you, so be even more hostile towards him, oppose him and do not believe the things with which he tries to tempt you.*

So the enmity is not something you are being asked to invent. It already exists, and it runs one way until you respond — he is at war with you whether or not you have noticed. The command is simply to stop being neutral. Note also what "taking him as an enemy" concretely consists of in Ibn Kathir's gloss: opposing him, and *not believing the things with which he tries to tempt you*. Enmity toward Shaytan is not mainly an emotion; it is a refusal to credit his suggestions.

**إِنَّمَا يَدْعُوا حِزْبَهُ لِيَكُونُوا مِنْ أَصْحَـٰبِ ٱلسَّعِيرِ** — "he only invites his party to be among the dwellers of the blazing Fire." He is a caller running an invitation of his own, and he has a *ḥizb* — a party, a faction, people enlisted on his side. Ibn Kathir strips away the packaging: he only wants to misguide you so that you will enter the blazing Fire with him. Whatever the invitation appears to offer, that is the destination printed on the ticket. Ibn Kathir sums him up in three words: *this is a manifest enemy.*

Ibn Kathir underlines the point with Surah al-Kahf (18:50), where after the angels prostrate to Adam and Iblis alone refuses — he was one of the Jinn and disobeyed the command of his Lord — Allah asks: "Will you then take him and his offspring as protectors and helpers rather than Me, while they are enemies to you? What an evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers." The bitter irony sits in the word *exchange*: to obey Shaytan is to swap the protection of your Lord for the friendship of one who is your declared enemy.

Ibn Kathir then makes a duʿā of his own — asking Allah, the All-Powerful and Almighty, to make us enemies of Shaytan and to make us followers of the Book of Allah and of the way of His Messengers, "for He is able to do whatever He wills and He will respond to all supplication." It is worth borrowing that duʿā, because the passage is not asking for a stance you can hold unaided.

## Ayah 7: the two lists

Ibn Kathir points out the join: having stated that the ultimate destiny of the followers of Iblis will be the blazing Fire, Allah then tells us the outcome for the two groups of people.

"Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment" — and Ibn Kathir gives the reason in one sentence: *this is because they obeyed the Shaytan and disobeyed Ar-Rahman.* That is the anatomy of disbelief as this passage frames it. It is not simply an error of opinion; it is having obeyed a caller who was announced as an enemy, in place of the Most Merciful.

"But those who believe and do righteous deeds will have forgiveness and a great reward." Ibn Kathir distinguishes the two gifts: the forgiveness is from whatever sins they did, and the great reward is for the good deeds that they did. So the believer is not being promised a spotless record — he is promised that the record's debts are cancelled and its credits are paid out generously. That is deliberate mercy in a passage about deception: the believer who has slipped is not in the enemy's camp, and *maghfirah* is named before the reward is.

## Ayah 8: when evil looks beautiful

**أَفَمَن زُيِّنَ لَهُۥ سُوٓءُ عَمَلِهِۦ فَرَءَاهُ حَسَنًا** — "Is he then, to whom the evil of his deeds is made fairseeming, so that he considers it as good…?" The verb is passive: the evil *is made* to seem fair to him. The one deceived does not experience it as deception at all. His sin does not feel like sin; it looks handsome to him. Read alongside Qurṭubī's explanation quoted at ayah 5, this is the finished product of the deceiver's work.

Ibn Kathir identifies who is meant: disbelievers or immoral persons who do evil deeds and believe that they are doing something good — and then he draws out the consequence for the Prophet ﷺ: a person who is like that has been misguided by Allah, "so what can you do for him? You cannot help him at all."

**فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُضِلُّ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهْدِى مَن يَشَآءُ** — "for Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills." Ibn Kathir explains this as being according to His decree, and immediately couples it with wisdom: Allah is Wise in His decree; He leaves astray whomsoever He leaves astray and guides whomsoever He guides, and in doing so He has perfect knowledge and wisdom. Guidance is not a commodity the caller can hand over; it is in the hand of Allah, given by His will, and His will is never blind.

**The occasion of these words.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Imam al-Baghawī relates, on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), that this statement — that Allah lets go astray whomsoever He wills and leads to the right path whomsoever He wills — was revealed at a time when the Prophet ﷺ had made the prayer: *"O Allah, bless Islam with prestige and power, through ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, or Abu Jahl."* Out of the two, Allah showed the right path to ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) and made him the cause of Islam's prestige and power, while Abu Jahl remained as astray as he was (Maʿārif cites this via Mazharī).

Sit with that for a moment. Two men were named in a single duʿā of the Prophet ﷺ. One becomes ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him). The other remains Abu Jahl. What separated them was not anything a human observer supplied — it was that Allah guided one of them, which is exactly the point of the ayah.

**فَلَا تَذْهَبْ نَفْسُكَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسَرَٰتٍ** — "so destroy not yourself in sorrow for them." It is the most tender line in the passage because of what it reveals about the one being addressed. Allah has to tell His Messenger ﷺ *not to destroy himself with grief* over people who called him a liar — which means that is precisely what he was inclined to do. This was not a man who wrote his opponents off; he ached for them.

Ibn Kathir's explanation is short: do not grieve about that, for Allah is Wise in His decree — He leaves astray whomsoever He leaves astray and guides whomsoever He guides, and in doing so He has perfect knowledge and wisdom. The relief here is relief from a burden you were never assigned. You are responsible for delivering, for calling, for making duʿā — but the outcome sits with Allah. To grieve yourself to pieces over a result that belongs to Him is, gently, to have misread your own job description.

And the closing seal: **إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ بِمَا يَصْنَعُونَ** — "truly Allah is the All-Knower of what they do." Nothing they are doing goes unobserved. Which brings us back to ayah 4: *and to Allah return all matters.* The passage begins and ends with the same assurance, and it is the assurance a hurt heart actually needs — not that the wrong did not happen, but that it is seen, and that it is His to settle.

## Living it

- **When you are rejected for your faith, remember whose road you are on** (ayah 4). Denial is the standing experience of those who carried this message, and the reckoning belongs to Allah.
- **Keep your sight trained on Allah alone** (ayah 4, with 35:2). Neither hope for benefit nor fear harm from anyone besides Him — Maʿārif calls this the antidote to thousands of anxieties.
- **Audit what is deceiving you** (ayah 5). One deception is the shine of this present life; the other is the chief deceiver's work on your view of Allah — persuading you that you are accepted while you sin.
- **Take the enemy as an enemy in the practical sense** (ayah 6): oppose him, and do not believe the things with which he tries to tempt you. Suspicion of the suggestion is worth more than indignation about Shaytan in the abstract.
- **Fear the moment your sin starts to look good to you** (ayah 8). Guard the ability to call a wrong a wrong; if that sense dulls, treat it as the alarm it is.
- **Do not treat anyone as beyond guidance** (ayah 8). Allah answered a duʿā that named two men, guiding one and leaving the other astray. Carry the message; hand the outcome back to Allah.

passages.title: The dead land revived and the word that ascends
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

These two ayat set two journeys side by side. In ayah 9, water travels **downward** — Allah sends the winds, the winds raise up the clouds, the clouds are driven to a dead land, and the land comes back to life; and that, Allah says, is exactly how the Resurrection will be. In ayah 10, words and deeds travel **upward** — the good word ascends to Allah, carried by righteous deeds, while the plotting of those who show off perishes.

What holds them together is a single argument about where real power lies. The One who can drive a rain cloud to a dead land and revive the earth after its death is the One who will raise the dead — and He is therefore the only place from which honour and power (*ʿizzah*) can be sought. Ayah 9 proves His power over dead matter; ayah 10 tells you what to do about it.

---

## Ayah 9: the argument you can walk out and see

**"And it is Allah Who sends the winds, so that they raise up the clouds, and We drive them to a dead land, and revive therewith the earth after its death. As such will be the Resurrection."**

Ibn Kathir opens by noting that Allah *often* refers to the Resurrection by using this very analogy — the earth coming back to life after it has died — and points to the beginning of Sūrat al-Ḥajj as the parallel, where Allah says of the dead earth that when rain comes down upon it, *"it is stirred (to life), and it swells and puts forth every lovely kind of growth"* (22:5).

Ibn Kathir's summary of the process is worth following step by step: the earth is dead and lifeless, with nothing growing in it; then He sends clouds to it; the clouds bring water; He sends the water down upon it — and the earth stirs, swells, and puts forth growth.

Notice how the ayah distributes the action. Allah *sends* the winds; the winds *raise up* the clouds; the clouds are then *driven* to their destination. Every link in that chain is ordinary and observable — wind, cloud, rain, shoots of green — and yet at every step Ibn Kathir names the Actor as Allah: *He* sends the clouds, *He* sends the water down upon it.

**"Such will be the Resurrection" (*ka-dhālika an-nushūr*).** Ibn Kathir spells out what the comparison amounts to: when Allah wishes to resurrect the bodies, He will send rain from beneath the Throne, which will cover the whole earth, and the bodies will grow in their graves like seeds grow in the earth.

That image of a seed is not decoration. Ibn Kathir immediately cites what is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ:

> *"Every part of the son of Adam will disintegrate apart from the coccyx — from it he was created, and from it he will be made anew."*

So the human being is, in this respect, genuinely like a seed: a small remainder stays in the ground, and from that remainder the whole is made anew. Ibn Kathir sets the two images side by side deliberately — the reviving land and the reviving body are not merely similar pictures, they are the same argument.

## Abu Razin's question — and how the Prophet ﷺ answered it

The most human moment in this passage comes from a report Ibn Kathir brings here. A man named Abu Razin asked: *"O Messenger of Allah, how will Allah bring the dead back to life? What is the sign of that in His creation?"*

The Prophet ﷺ did not answer with an argument. He answered with a memory Abu Razin already had:

> *"O Abu Razin, do you not pass through the valley of your people and see it arid and barren, then pass through it again and see it stirred to life and green?"*

"Yes," he said.

> *"Thus will Allah bring the dead back to life."*

(Ibn Kathir introduces this simply as "the Ḥadīth of Abu Razin". The source before us does not name the collection it comes from, so we will not name one either.)

Two things are worth sitting with. First, notice that Ibn Kathir describes Abu Razin's valley in exactly the words he had just used for the earth in 22:5 — both are *"stirred (to life)"*. The sign in the ayah and the sign in the valley are the same event. Second — and this is the pedagogical heart of ayah 9 — the sign Abu Razin asked for was not something exotic. It was his own valley, seen twice. Ibn Kathir's phrase for what Allah is doing here is that He *urges His servants to draw the lesson of the former from the latter*: to reason from the reviving they have already witnessed to the one they have not.

---

## Ayah 10: whoever desires ʿizzah

**"Whosoever desires al-ʿizzah — then to Allah belongs all al-ʿizzah."**

*ʿIzzah* is a word English has to render with more than one: the translation of the ayah in front of us gives "honour and power", while Ibn Kathir's rendering has "honour, power and glory". Everyone wants it. The ayah does not scold the desire — it redirects it.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as an implied instruction: whoever desires honour, power and glory in this world and the next, **let him be obedient towards Allah**. That obedience "will help him reach his goal, for Allah is the Sovereign of this world and the Hereafter, and to Him belong all honour, power and glory." Ibn Kathir returns to the point a second time in case it is missed: the ayah means *let him seek honour, power and glory through obeying Allah*.

He then places three other ayat alongside it, and together they map the whole error:

- **4:139** — *"Those who take disbelievers for protectors instead of believers: do they seek al-ʿizzah with them? Verily, to Allah belongs all honour, power and glory."* Seeking standing by attaching yourself to the wrong party.
- **10:65** — *"And let not their speech grieve you; all al-ʿizzah belongs to Allah."* What people say about you is not where honour is kept.
- **63:8** — *"But al-ʿizzah belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers — but the hypocrites know not."* Here is the resolution: *ʿizzah* is entirely Allah's, and it reaches His Messenger ﷺ and the believers from Him. On Ibn Kathir's reading of our ayah, the road to it is obedience — which is to say it is granted, not seized.

**Mujahid** read the opening clause as aimed at a specific target: "whosoever desires al-ʿizzah" — that is, by worshipping idols — "then to Allah belongs all al-ʿizzah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point in wider terms, and it is worth quoting the shape of it: honour and power "are not controlled by anyone other than Allah." As for those who have taken certain things as objects of worship, or have taken certain people as friends in the hope of being honoured by them — *they cannot give honour to anyone.* You may spend a lifetime cultivating a party that has nothing to give.

---

## The word that ascends, and what carries it

**"To Him ascend the good words, and the righteous deeds exalt it."**

**What is "the good word"?** Ibn Kathir: words of remembrance (*dhikr*), recitation of the Qur'an, and supplications — "this was the view of more than one of the Salaf." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the first and greatest of them: the *kalimah* of *tawḥīd*, *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, together with knowledge of Allah's being and attributes.

**Where does it go?** Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Jarīr, via al-Mukhāriq ibn Sulaym, that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said to his companions: "If we tell you a ḥadīth, we will bring you proof of it from the Book of Allah." Then he described it: when the Muslim servant says *"Glory and praise be to Allah, there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, Allah is Most Great, and blessed be Allah"* — an angel takes those words and puts them under his wing, then ascends with them to the heaven; and he does not take them past any group of angels but they seek forgiveness for the one who said them, until he brings them before Allah. And then Ibn Masʿūd recited this very ayah as his proof.

Ibn Kathir also records from Imām Aḥmad, on the authority of an-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that those who remember Allah — glorifying Him, magnifying Him, praising Him and declaring His oneness — those words *"go around the Throne buzzing like bees, mentioning those who said them. Would one of you not like to have something with Allah mentioning him?"* Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Ibn Mājah.

Take the image seriously and gently. We affirm the Throne as Allah has affirmed it, without likening it to anything in creation and without emptying the word of its meaning. What the ḥadīth gives you is this: the *dhikr* you say quietly, in a car or a kitchen, does not evaporate. It ascends, it keeps sounding, and it keeps naming you.

## "And the righteous deed exalts it" — the grammar that decides the meaning

The clause *wa-l-ʿamalu-ṣ-ṣāliḥu yarfaʿuh* contains pronouns that could point in either of two directions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says so plainly — in this grammatical arrangement "there are certain probabilities", and the meaning of the sentence changes with each — and then lays both out rather than choosing for you.

**Reading one (the majority).** The one doing the lifting is *the righteous deed*, and the thing lifted is *the good word*: good words ascend to Allah, and the thing through which they are made to ascend is good deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this as the rendering in the *khulāṣa* of Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī, and as the choice of the majority of the authorities in tafsīr — Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mujāhid, Ḍaḥḥāk, Shahr ibn Ḥawshab and others.

**Reading two.** Some commentators reverse the pronouns: the *good word* — the *dhikr* of Allah — is what lifts the *righteous deed* and raises it higher, making it worthy of being accepted. On this reading, a person who does good deeds and also keeps up abundant *dhikr* finds that his remembrance of Allah embellishes his deeds and makes them acceptable.

**Why this matters.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that "ascending" and "being helped to ascend" mean *being accepted in the sight of Allah*. So on the majority reading the gist is: no good word — be it the *kalimah* of *tawḥīd* or any other words of remembrance and glorification of Allah — gets to be acceptable with Allah without good deed. Words are not self-validating.

Ibn Kathir preserves a sharper version of the same idea from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), reported by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah: "The good word is the remembrance of Allah, which is taken up to Allah, and the righteous deed is the performance of the obligatory duties. Whoever remembers Allah when doing an obligatory duty, his deed carries his remembrance of Allah and takes it up to Allah. Whoever remembers Allah and does not perform the obligatory duties, his words will be rejected, as will his deed."

Read that twice. The obligatory duties are the vehicle. *Dhikr* on the tongue of someone who has abandoned what Allah made obligatory has nothing to ride on.

**How far does the warning go?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and the distinctions are worth keeping straight:

- Faith and its confirmation in the heart — belief in Allah's Oneness — is a **necessary condition** for the acceptance of deeds in the absolute sense. Without it, however many times a person repeats the *kalimah* and however much *dhikr* and *tasbīḥ* he engages in, he will not deserve the least acceptability in the sight of Allah.
- The other parts of good deed — prayers, fasting, abstinence from what is forbidden and reprehensible — are conditions of **perfect** acceptability. The acceptability of the "good word" itself does not depend on them; a person who genuinely has faith but fails in other deeds or falls short in them has not said the *kalimah* in vain — but its benefit will be restricted to delivering him from the everlasting punishment, and he will go through punishment for some time, in proportion to what he abandoned and fell short in.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds one more condition, citing through Qurṭubī a ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah does not accept any word without deed, nor any word and deed without the intention, nor any word, deed and intention without compatibility with the Sunnah. Four things, then, and the last is easy to forget: word, deed, intention — and doing it the way he ﷺ did it. Even if word, deed and intention are all correct, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, a mode of conduct out of step with the Sunnah falls short of perfect acceptability.

**The tested prescription.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Shāh ʿAbdul Qādir in *Mūḍiḥ ul-Qurʼān* that this prescription for becoming a recipient of honour is perfectly true and tested — on one condition: **constancy**. One must remain constant in remembering Allah and in doing good deeds; and when that constancy reaches an appointed limit, Allah blesses the doer with an everlasting and unparalleled honour, both in this world and in the world to come.

So ayah 10 is not only a description of how worship travels; it is the answer to the question the ayah opens with. You wanted *ʿizzah*? This is the road.

---

## The counter-movement: those who plot

**"But those who plot evils — theirs will be a severe torment, and the plotting of such will perish."**

Ibn Kathir reports that **Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab** said this refers to **those who show off by their actions** — that is, they deceive the people by giving the impression that they are obeying Allah, when in fact they are hated by Allah for showing off.

Set this against the first half of the ayah and the passage snaps into focus. Two people may say identical words and perform identical acts. One person's words are taken up by an angel and carried past ranks of angels who ask forgiveness for him; the other person's identical words are classified as *makr* — plotting. The difference is not in the vocabulary but in who the performance is aimed at.

Ibn Kathir explains why such scheming is doomed: it "will fail and vanish, for their reality is apparent from up close to those who have insight and wisdom. No one conceals a secret but Allah will cause it to become known, on his face or by a slip of the tongue, or He will cause the person to wear it like a cloak. If it is good, then the consequences will be good, and if it is bad, then the consequences will be bad." The one who shows off, he adds, cannot continue to deceive anyone but the fool; the believers who have insight are not deceived — from up close, they soon discover it. And nothing at all can be hidden from the Knower of the Unseen.

That last line is where ayah 10 rejoins ayah 9. The One who drives a cloud to a dead land and grows bodies in their graves like seeds in the earth is not a Lord who can be managed by impression-making.

---

## Living these two ayat

**Look at the world as evidence, not scenery.** Ayah 9 asks you to do what the Prophet ﷺ asked Abu Razin to do: recall a place you have seen barren and then seen green, and let that settle the question of whether Allah can raise you. Ibn Kathir's word for it is that Allah *urges His servants to draw the lesson of the former from the latter*.

**Redirect the desire for standing rather than killing it.** You are allowed to want *ʿizzah*. Ibn Kathir's answer is that all of it belongs to Allah, and the way to it is obedience to Him — not, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, attaching yourself to people in the hope of being honoured by them, when they cannot give honour to anyone.

**Bind your *dhikr* to your obligations.** On Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, remembrance is carried up by the performance of the obligatory duties. The practical form of this is unglamorous: pray what you owe, keep away from what is forbidden, and let your *tasbīḥ* live inside that structure rather than instead of it.

**Be constant.** Shāh ʿAbdul Qādir's condition is not intensity but constancy — remembrance and good deeds kept up until they reach their appointed limit.

**And check the audience.** Every act in this passage travels in one of two directions. Sincere words ascend and go around the Throne, mentioning the one who said them. The same words, performed to give people an impression, are *makr* — and Allah says of it, plainly, *it will perish*.

passages.title: Dust, sea, and sky: the idols who own nothing
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a single question: who actually owns and runs this world? Ayah 11 takes you back to dust and a drop of fluid and into the secrecy of the womb; ayah 12 spreads out the two kinds of water; ayah 13 sets night, day, sun and moon turning on their appointed courses. Then the verdict lands: **"Such is Allah, your Lord; His is the kingdom"** — and the beings people call on beside Him "own not even a *qitmir*" (13), cannot hear you (14), and will disown you on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir's own headings over this material track the movement: he heads the first part *"Allah is the Creator and Knower of the Unseen,"* the middle *"The Blessings and Signs of Allah,"* and the last *"The gods of the Idolators do not even own a Qitmir."*

## Dust, a drop, and a pair

The passage opens where every human being begins. Ibn Kathir separates the two stages carefully: **"He initiated the creation of your father Adam from dust, then He created his offspring from semen of worthless water."** *Turāb* — dust, dry earth — names the origin of the first human; *nuṭfah*, the small drop of fluid, names the origin of everyone since. Both are deliberately unimpressive materials.

That matters, because Ibn Kathir has just been discussing resurrection under the heading *"Evidence of Life after Death"* — how Allah often points to the earth coming back to life after it has died as the lesson for the raising of the dead. When Allah wishes to resurrect the bodies, Ibn Kathir writes, "He will send rain from beneath the Throne which will cover the whole earth, and the bodies will grow in their graves like seeds grow in the earth." He cites there a hadith found in the Sahih: **"Every part of the son of Adam will disintegrate apart from the coccyx, from which he was created and from him he will be made anew."** And he relates the hadith of Abū Razīn, who asked, "O Messenger of Allah, how will Allah bring the dead back to life? What is the sign of that in His creation?" The Prophet ﷺ answered by pointing him at something he had already seen with his own eyes: **"O Abu Razin, do you not pass through the valley of your people (and see it) arid and barren, then you pass through it (and see it) stirred (to life) and green?"** He said, "Yes." He ﷺ said: **"Thus will Allah bring the dead back to life."** A being made from dust, told to look at a valley he has watched turn green, has no grounds for finding resurrection hard to believe.

Then comes a turn of tone easy to read past: **"then He made you pairs."** Ibn Kathir's comment is unexpectedly tender — male and female, "as a kindness and a mercy from Him, He gave you partners from your own kind, that you may find repose in them." So the ayah is not a cold inventory of biological stages. It moves from dust, to a drop, to the settled companionship of a marriage — three steps none of us arranged for ourselves.

## Knowledge where ours ends

**"And no female conceives or gives birth but with His knowledge."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: "He knows about that and nothing is hidden from Him at all." Pregnancy is the human situation in which knowledge is most obviously *not* ours — hidden, interior, unpredictable. The Qur'an chooses precisely that to name as fully open to Allah.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two ayat that widen the point: "not a leaf falls, but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record" (6:59), and "Allah knows what every female bears, and by how much the wombs fall short or exceed. Everything with Him is in (due) proportion. All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Most Great, the Most High" (13:8–9). Notice the pattern: Allah's knowledge is not a vague awareness of generalities but a written, itemised, exact record — down to a single falling leaf and a seed buried in the dark.

## "Nor is a part cut off from his life": two readings

**"And no aged man is granted a length of life nor is a part cut off from his life, but is in a Book."** Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pause here, because the early commentators genuinely read this clause two ways.

**The majority view.** The ayah is not about one individual's span lengthening or shortening, but about humankind as a class: some are given long lives, others short ones, and every one of those spans already stands recorded. Ibn Kathir's gloss on the first clause is that some are "granted a long life, which He knows and it is recorded with Him in the First Book"; and on the second he notes that "his" here "refers to mankind in general, not to a specific person, because the long life which is recorded in the Book and is known by Allah will not be cut off." He reports from Ibn ʿAbbās (via al-ʿAwfī): "There is no one for whom Allah has decreed a long life but he will reach the age that has been decreed for him. When he reaches the time that has been decreed for him, he will not surpass it. And there is no one for whom Allah has decreed a short life but it will end when he reaches the age that has been decreed for him" — "that is recorded in a Book with Him." Ad-Daḥḥāk bin Muzāḥim held the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the recording in *al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet, adds that Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ reports the same saying from Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Daḥḥāk, and notes that the general works of tafsir — Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Kathir, Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and others — declare this the position of the majority of commentators.

**The other reading.** Some early commentators took "his life" to mean one particular person: the total is already fixed and written, and what "is cut off" is the remainder — "his time is constantly decreasing," as Ibn Kathir puts it, "known to Allah year after year, month after month, week after week, day after day, hour after hour. Everything is written with Allah in His Book." Ibn Jarīr reports this from Abū Mālik; it was also the view of as-Suddī and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same explanation from Shaʿbī, Ibn Jubayr, Abū Mālik, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Suddiyy (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī), and quotes an Arabic couplet that compresses the idea:

> Your life is (the name of) counted breaths. So, whenever passes away a breath from it, a part of it decreases.

Neither reading threatens the other's core: in both, nothing about your lifespan is loose or accidental. The difference is only where the accounting is placed — across humanity, or inside one person's ledger of breaths.

## The one deed the Sunnah attaches here

Both commentaries bring the same hadith at this ayah. In his tafsir of it, Imam an-Nasāʾī records from Anas bin Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: **"Whoever would like to have ample provision and a long life, let him uphold the ties of kinship."** Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Abū Dāwūd.

That raises an obvious question against the ayah: if the term is written, how does keeping family ties *increase* it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers with a second narration, which Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports from Abū ad-Dardāʾ (may Allah be pleased with him): when this was mentioned before the Prophet ﷺ, he explained that age is already fixed and determined by Allah, and when the fixed term is over no one is given the least respite; the "increase" means that Allah blesses such a person with good children who keep praying for him, so that he continues to receive their prayers in his grave. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up: reports that certain deeds cause age to increase mean an increase in the *barakah* — the blessing, the bliss — of that life.

So the clause about written lifespans is not an invitation to fatalism. The Sunnah attaches it directly to going and repairing things with your relatives.

**"Surely, that is easy for Allah."** Ibn Kathir: "that is very easy for Him, and He has detailed knowledge of all His creation, for His knowledge encompasses all things, and nothing at all is hidden from Him." Tracking every conception, every birth, every span of every life is no strain for Allah — it is *yasīr*, easy.

## Signs you can drink, sail, and watch

Ayat 12 and 13 do one job together: they take things so ordinary that nobody notices them and show them as owned, driven, and maintained. Ibn Kathir opens the section by saying Allah is here "pointing out His mighty power in creating different things."

**"And the two seas are not alike: this is palatable, sweet and pleasant to drink, and that is salty and bitter."** Ibn Kathir identifies them concretely. The sweet water is the rivers "which flow among people, rivers great and small according to people's needs in all regions and areas and lands" — "sweet and palatable for whoever wants to drink it." The salty is "unpalatable... the ocean in which the big ships sail, and is salty and undrinkable." Two utterly different substances, each suited to a different human need: one you drink, one you sail. The difference itself is the sign.

And then both are shown to be generous in the same two ways.

**"And from them both you eat fresh tender meat"** — Ibn Kathir: fish. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches a legal point in the wording. By alluding to fish as *laḥm*, meat, the ayah hints that this is meat already lawful in itself: unlike land animals, which do not become halal unless slaughtered with the name of Allah, fish carries no such condition. It is "meat, ready to eat."

**"and derive the ornaments that you wear"** — *ḥilyah*, ornament, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says refers to pearls; Ibn Kathir compares "Out of them both come out pearl and coral. Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?" (55:22–23). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah says *from both* waters, against the general belief that pearls come only from the brackish water of the seas; the reality, it says, is what is evident from the words of the Qur'an — they form in both, much less in sweet water and far more in the brackish. It adds (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī) that the masculine form in *talbasūnahā*, "that you wear," hints that pearls are permissible for men as well — contrary to gold and silver, whose use as an ornament is not permissible for men.

**"And you see the ships cleaving"** — *mawākhir*: they travel through it, Ibn Kathir explains, "plowing through the water with their beak-shaped bows." Mujāhid observed that the wind drives the ships, "and the wind cannot drive any ships except the big ones." **"That you may seek of His bounty"** means trade — "through your journeys to engage in trade from one land to another." And **"that you may give thanks"** means, in Ibn Kathir's phrasing, thanks "to your Lord for subjugating this mighty creation – the sea – to you, so that you can travel through it as you wish and go wherever you want, and nothing stops you; His power has subjugated for you whatever is in the heavens and on earth, and all of this is by His grace and mercy."

Then the same demonstration moves upward. Introducing ayah 13, Ibn Kathir writes: "Another aspect of His perfect power and might is that He has subjugated the night with its darkness and the day with its light." **"He merges the night into the day, and He merges the day into the night"** describes a continual transfer: "He takes from the length of the one and adds it to the shortness of the other, until they become equal. Then He takes from the latter and adds to the former, so one becomes long and the other becomes short, so they take from one another in summer and in winter." The lengthening and shortening of the day across a year is not an accident of geometry; it is an act, being done, by One who is doing it.

**"And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each runs its course for a term appointed."** Ibn Kathir includes the stars and planets with their light: "All of them run in their appointed courses and in the manner prescribed for them, as decreed by the Almighty, All-Knowing" — and *for a term appointed*, he says, means until the Day of Resurrection. Even the sun is on a schedule that ends.

## The verdict, and a thread off a date stone

Now the passage turns. **"Such is Allah, your Lord; His is the kingdom"** — Ibn Kathir: "the One Who has done all this is the Almighty Lord besides Whom there is no other true deity." Everything since ayah 11 has been evidence for this one sentence.

**"And those whom you invoke instead of Him own not even a *qitmir*."** Ibn Kathir identifies the target: the idols and false gods "whom you claim to be in the form of angels who are close to Allah" — not crude stone-worship in the worshippers' own minds, but beings imagined as intermediaries with influence at the highest court.

And what do they own? Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAṭiyah al-ʿAwfī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others all explain *qitmīr* as **"the thread that is attached to the pit of a date."** Ibn Kathir spells out the force of it: "they do not possess anything in the heavens or on earth, not even anything equivalent to this qitmir." Set that against what has just been described — rivers, oceans, pearls, ships, sun, moon, the turning of night and day, all owned and driven by Allah — and the contrast is total: everything, against a thread off a date stone.

## Three failures

Ayah 14 dismantles the false god in three moves, in the order a desperate person would experience them.

**First, they cannot hear.** "If you invoke them, they hear not your call" — Ibn Kathir: the gods you call on instead of Allah "do not hear your supplication, because they are inanimate and have no soul in them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the reasoning to the harder case: someone might call not on a statue but on a prophet or an angel taken as a god. Such beings do possess the ability to hear — "yet they are not present everywhere nor do they hear that which is said by everybody." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes in passing that the separate question of whether the dead can hear, *samāʿ al-mawtā*, is neither confirmed nor rejected by this ayah; the arguments and proofs on that are different, and it treats them under Sūrah ar-Rūm.)

**Second, even supposing they heard, they could not act.** "And if they were to hear, they could not grant it to you" — Ibn Kathir: "they are not able to do any of the things that you ask them for." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the decisive reason: "they themselves have no control over it, and cannot intercede with Allah on behalf of anyone without His permission." This is where the intercession theory collapses. The whole appeal of a lesser deity is a shortcut — a being with leverage. The ayah answers that there is no leverage to have.

**Third, they will turn on you.** "And on the Day of Resurrection, they will disown your worshipping them" — which Ibn Kathir renders plainly: "they will disown you." He brings two parallels: "And when mankind are gathered, they (false deities) will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping" (46:5–6), and "And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might give them honor, power and glory. Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them" (19:81–82). That second ayah names the motive exactly: people reach for these beings hoping to gain standing and power, *ʿizzah*, through them. So the transaction fails at both ends — nothing is gained now, and on the Day of Resurrection the supposed patron becomes the opponent.

## "And none can inform you like Him Who is the All-Knower"

The closing clause is the passage's guarantee. The word rendered "the All-Knower" here is *Khabīr*, and Ibn Kathir's gloss stays with what the ayah is doing: "no one can tell you about the consequences of things and how they will end like the One Who is the All-Knower of them." Qatādah said Allah "is referring to Himself, may He be blessed and exalted, for He undoubtedly tells the truth."

Everything the passage has claimed depends on knowledge no created being has: what happens in a womb, how long a life runs, what an idol is actually worth, what will be said on the Day of Resurrection. On all of it you have the report of the One who knows how things end — which is why the believer can take its verdict about the false gods as settled rather than probable.

**Living it.** Two concrete things follow. Take every request straight to Allah, since anything else in the chain neither hears nor can act. And go mend the ties with your relatives — the one practical deed the Sunnah attaches to this passage about written lifespans, with the promise of ample provision and *barakah* in the life you have been given.

passages.title: Humanity's utter need of the Self-Sufficient
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set two facts side by side: right now, every human being is utterly dependent on Allah while He needs no one; and on the Day of Resurrection, that same aloneness will be laid bare, when no soul can carry any part of another's load. What holds the passage together is a single question — **who can actually help you?** Ayah 15 answers it about this life, ayah 18 answers it about the next, and ayat 16–17 stand between them as the reminder that our very continuation is on loan.

## What the passage is answering

The ayah immediately before this passage (35:14) had just dismantled the whole business of calling on anything besides Allah in a crisis: *"If you call them, they do not hear your call, and even if they were to hear, they would not respond to you."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks that carefully, because it matters for what follows. If you call upon idols, or upon prophets or angels taken as gods and worshipped, asking them to help you in distress — idols cannot listen to you at all, because they do not have the ability to listen. Prophets and angels do have that ability, yet they are not present everywhere, nor do they hear all that is said by everybody. And even supposing, for the sake of argument, that they did hear — as in the case of angels and prophets — they still would not fulfil the request, because they themselves have no control over it, and they cannot intercede with Allah on behalf of anyone without His permission.

(Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise note here: the separate scholarly question of *samāʿ al-mawtā*, whether the dead can hear, is neither confirmed nor rejected by this ayah. The arguments and proofs relating to that question are of a different kind, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it in detail in its commentary on Sūrah ar-Rūm.)

So the ground is cleared. Every door has been shown to be shut except one. And it is exactly at that point that ayah 15 turns and addresses the whole of humanity.

## Ayah 15: you are the ones in need

**يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ أَنتُمُ الْفُقَرَاءُ إِلَى اللَّهِ**
*"O humanity! It is you who stand in need of Allah."*

Notice who is being addressed: **an-nās** — humanity, all of it. And Ibn Kathir opens the passage by widening the frame even further than that: Allah is telling us here that **He has no need of anyone or anything else, but all of creation is in need of Him and is in a position of humility before Him.**

That last phrase is worth sitting with. Creation is not merely *dependent* on Allah as a bare fact; it stands in a position of humility before Him. Need is not an accident that befell us — it is our standing.

Then Ibn Kathir explains the phrase itself in one clean stroke: **they need Him in all that they do, but He has no need of them at all.** Not in most of what they do — in all of it. The neediness the ayah names (*al-fuqarāʾ*, those in need) is not a social class or a bad season. It is the human condition as such.

**وَاللَّهُ هُوَ الْغَنِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ**
*"But Allah is the Rich, Worthy of all praise."*

Two of Allah's names close the ayah, and they are joined for a reason.

**al-Ghanī** — the Rich, the One free of all need. Ibn Kathir: **He is unique in His being Free of all needs, and has no partner or associate.** Self-sufficiency is not something Allah has more of than others; it is His alone. Everything else in existence stands on the other side of that line, among those in need.

**al-Ḥamīd** — Worthy of all praise. Ibn Kathir says: worthy of all praise **in all that He does, says, decrees and legislates**. Those four words cover everything a servant could ever have a complaint about. What He *does*, what He *says*, what He *decrees* for your life, and what He *legislates* as law — praise is due in every one of those, not only in the parts you enjoy.

Pairing the two names is the mercy of the ayah. A self-sufficient power who was not praiseworthy would be terrifying to depend on. A praiseworthy being who was needy could not carry your weight. Only *al-Ghanī al-Ḥamīd* is both able to be leaned on entirely and good enough to deserve it.

## Ayat 16–17: you are not indispensable

**إِن يَشَأْ يُذْهِبْكُم وَيَأْتِ بِخَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ ۝ وَمَا ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ بِعَزِيزٍ**
*"If He willed, He could eliminate you and produce a new creation. And that is not difficult for Allah at all."*

If ayah 15 stated our poverty, these two ayat press it home in the most direct way available: by pointing at our continued existence and noting that it rests entirely on His will.

Ibn Kathir's comment is spare: **if He wanted to, He could destroy you and bring forth another people, and this is not difficult or impossible for Him.**

Read the two ayat as one sentence and the psychology of it becomes clear. A tyrant needs his subjects — his power is made of them, so he cannot afford to lose them. Allah is not in that position. The human race is not load-bearing. And ayah 17 closes off the last escape a proud heart might reach for: perhaps He *tolerates* us because replacing us would be costly. No — as Ibn Kathir puts it, this is neither difficult nor impossible for Him.

This is ayah 15 turned around. There, you were told you need Him in everything. Here, you are told He needs you in nothing. Which means every moment of being alive is a gift and not a wage.

## Ayah 18: the load nobody else will carry

**وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ**
*"No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another."*

Ibn Kathir specifies the setting in three words: **on the Day of Resurrection.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in plain terms — on the Day of Judgment, no one will be able to bear the burden of another person's sins; everyone will have to bear his or her own burden.

**وَإِن تَدْعُ مُثْقَلَةٌ إِلَىٰ حِمْلِهَا لَا يُحْمَلْ مِنْهُ شَيْءٌ وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَىٰ**
*"and if one heavily laden calls another to bear his load, nothing of it will be lifted even though he be near of kin."*

Ibn Kathir reads the appeal carefully: **if the person who is carrying a heavy burden calls someone else to help him carry his load, all or part of it** — and the ayah's answer refuses even the partial request. Not the whole load, and not part of it: *nothing* of it will be lifted.

Then comes the detail that turns the ayah personal. **"Even though he be near of kin"** — Ibn Kathir says: **even if he is closely related to him, even if he is his father or son, for each person will be preoccupied with his own self and his own situation.** Not because love has died on that Day, but because everyone will be entirely absorbed in their own standing before Allah.

### ʿIkrimah's scene at the Reckoning

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records how Sayyidnā ʿIkrimah (may Allah be pleased with him) explained this ayah, and it is the most vivid thing in the whole passage.

On that Day a father says to his son: *"You know how affectionate a father I was to you?"* The son answers: *"Yes — your favours to me are countless. You have certainly faced many a hardship for me during the life of the world."* So the father says: *"Son, today I need you. Give me some of your good deeds, so that I can have my salvation."* And the son replies: *"Father, the return you asked for is not much, but what can I do? If I were to give that to you, I shall be facing the same situation that you are facing now; therefore, I am sorry, I cannot help you."*

The father then turns to his wife with the same plea — *"I sacrificed everything for you during the life of the world. Today, I need a few of your good deeds"* — and receives the same answer.

This, ʿIkrimah said, is what *"no bearer will bear the burden of another"* means. The debt is acknowledged. The affection is denied by no one in the scene. And still nothing moves across.

### The other ayat on the same theme

ʿIkrimah went on to note that the Qur'an takes up this subject in several of its ayat — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Ibn Kathir as its source for this:

- On that Day, neither would a father be able to have his son spared from the punishment, nor would a son be able to do that for his father (31:33).
- On that Day, one will run from his brother, and his mother and father, and his wife and children (80:34–35). And the reason for the running, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is fear: lest these people try to pass the burden of their sins on to him, or come to him with a request for some of his good deeds.

The essential sense, it concludes, is that **no one will save another person by carrying the burden of his sins over one's own shoulders.**

But it then adds a careful and important qualification: **the matter of intercession (*shafāʿah*) is different.** The ayah shuts the door on transferring guilt; it does not deny intercession, which stands on another footing entirely — and recall from the previous ayah that no one intercedes with Allah without His permission.

### A resolved difficulty

There is an apparent tension here that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises and settles, quoting *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt (29:13) says that those who make others go astray will bear not only the burden of having gone astray themselves, but also the burden of having made others go astray. If no one bears another's load, how can they be carrying loads on top of their own?

The resolution: this does not mean they somehow lighten the burden of those they caused to go astray. That burden stays exactly where it was, in its own place, on them. Rather, the crime of the one who misleads is itself twofold — first that he was astray, and second that he made others go astray — so his burden too becomes twofold, for his *own* two offences. There is no contradiction between the two ayat. Nobody's account is being lightened; a second account is simply being charged to the person who earned it.

## Who the warning actually reaches

**إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ الَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُم بِالْغَيْبِ وَأَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ**
*"You can warn only those who fear their Lord unseen and perform the Salah."*

Having laid out the reckoning, the passage turns to the Prophet ﷺ and tells him where his warning will land. Ibn Kathir paraphrases it: *the only ones who will draw a lesson from what you have brought are those who are possessed of insight and wisdom, who fear their Lord and who do as He commands.*

Two marks are named, one inward and one outward: they **fear their Lord**, and they **establish the prayer**. In Ibn Kathir's reading the two belong together — those who fear their Lord *and who do as He commands*. Inward awe that never becomes an outward standing in prayer is not what this ayah describes.

There is something quietly humbling in the "only" of *innamā*. The Messenger ﷺ delivered the warning perfectly, and still it took root only in prepared hearts. So when truth is being spoken and someone is unmoved, the failure is not always in the speaking.

## The last word: your purification is your own gain

**وَمَن تَزَكَّىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِ ۖ وَإِلَى اللَّهِ الْمَصِيرُ**
*"And he who purifies himself, then he purifies only for the benefit of himself. And to Allah is the Return."*

*Tazakkā* — to purify oneself; Ibn Kathir's rendering of the ayah spells out the scope, purification *from all kinds of sins*. And he explains the phrase as meaning **one who does righteous deeds: the benefit of that will come back to him.**

This is the exact mirror of the burden clause, which is why both sit in the same ayah. Just as no one can take your load off you, no one can take your reward from you. The ledger that cannot be shared in loss also cannot be raided in gain. And it answers ayah 15 too: since Allah is *al-Ghanī*, free of all need, your purification adds nothing to Him — the whole profit is yours.

**وَإِلَى اللَّهِ الْمَصِيرُ** — *"And to Allah is the Return."* Ibn Kathir: **to Him everything will ultimately return, and He is swift in bringing to account. He will reward or punish everyone according to his deeds: if they are good, then the end will be good, and if they are bad, then the end will be bad.**

## Living it

The passage is not abstract theology; it is a redirection of where a person turns.

**Take your need where it can be met.** Ayah 15 does not scold you for being needy — it names need as your permanent condition and then names the only One who is free of it. The mistake is never in asking; it is in asking at a door that cannot hear, or cannot respond, or has no authority to grant.

**Praise Him in the decree, not only in the gift.** Ibn Kathir tied *al-Ḥamīd* to all that Allah does, says, decrees and legislates. That is a standard for a believer's speech in hard seasons.

**Let ayat 16–17 cure any sense of being owed.** He could bring forth another people, and it would be neither difficult nor impossible for Him. Nothing you do for Allah is a favour to Him.

**Work as though you will stand alone, because you will.** Read ʿIkrimah's scene and let it correct the quiet assumption that righteous parents, a devout spouse, or pious children are a form of savings. Nobody in that scene is unkind. There is simply nothing to hand over.

**And build the two marks named in ayah 18.** Fear of your Lord, and a prayer you actually establish — the marks Ibn Kathir links to insight and wisdom, and to doing as Allah commands. Those are what the ayah says make a person capable of hearing a warning at all — and every bit of that purification, the ayah promises, comes back to you.

passages.title: The blind and the seeing are not alike
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In four short strokes — the blind and the seeing, darkness and light, shade and the sun's heat, the living and the dead — Allah refuses to let faith and disbelief be treated as two comparable things. Then, having drawn the gap, He tells His Prophet ﷺ where the power to close it actually lies: hearing that benefits a person is given by Allah, and the Messenger's own task is to convey and to warn.

**What holds ayat 19–23 together.** Ibn Kathir takes this run as one connected passage, and the logic is tight. Ayat 19–22a pile up the contrasts; the end of ayah 22 and ayah 23 draw the conclusion. If the two parties are as far apart as a living man and a corpse, then making the second into the first is not the Messenger's doing — "Verily, Allah makes whom He wills to hear" — and so the word to him is: "You are only a warner."

## Four pairs, one point

**"Not alike are the blind and the seeing"** (ayah 19). Ibn Kathir's comment is plain: Allah says that these antonyms "are clearly not equal, the blind and the seeing are not equal, there is a difference and a huge gap between them." Note the shape of the statement. It is not "the blind man is worse"; it is that the two are not equal — the comparison itself is refused.

**Darkness and light** (ayah 20), **shade and the sun's heat** (ayah 21). Ibn Kathir continues in the same breath: "Darkness and light are not equal, neither are shade and the sun's heat." The translation before us renders the third pair as the scorching heat and the cool shade; Ibn Kathir's wording is "the sun's heat." Each pair is another form of the same denial, laid one on top of the other.
