**The living and the dead** (ayah 22). Here Ibn Kathir tells us what all of it is a picture of: "By the same token, the living and the dead are not equal. This is the parable Allah makes of the believers who are the living, and the disbelievers who are the dead." He supports the reading from the Qur'an itself — "Is he who was dead and We gave him life and set for him a light whereby he can walk amongst men — like him who is in the depths of darkness from which he can never come out?" (6:122), and "The parable of the two parties is as that of the blind and the deaf and the seer and the hearer. Are they equal when compared?" (11:24).

## Ibn Kathir's two journeys

The most striking thing in this commentary is that Ibn Kathir does not leave these opposites as abstractions. He runs them out into two whole lives, this world and the next, and the images of ayat 19–22 each find a place:

> The believer sees and hears, and walks in the light upon a straight path in this world and the Hereafter, until he comes to settle in Gardens wherein is shade and springs. The disbeliever is blind and deaf, walking in darkness from which he cannot escape, he is lost in his misguidance in this world and the Hereafter, until he ends up in fierce hot wind and boiling water, and shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor good.

Look at what he has done with the pairs. The *seeing* of ayah 19 becomes a man who can see the road. The *light* of ayah 20 is what he walks by. The *shade* of ayah 21 becomes the shade of the Gardens where he finally settles — and the heat of that same ayah becomes the fierce hot wind and boiling water at the other end. Even the counterfeit is accounted for: the disbeliever has a "shadow" too, but it is the shadow of black smoke, "neither cool nor good."

So on Ibn Kathir's reading the four pairs are not four unrelated comparisons. They are one road described from several sides: the eye, the light on the path, and where the traveller comes to rest. And notice that in his picture the disbeliever is not simply someone holding a wrong opinion. He is a man walking — "in darkness from which he cannot escape."

## "Verily, Allah makes whom He wills to hear"

The turn comes at the end of ayah 22. Ibn Kathir explains "Verily, Allah makes whom He wills to hear" as meaning that "He guides them to listen to the proof and accept it and adhere" to it. Hearing here is not the ear working. It is a chain: listening, accepting, holding fast — and Ibn Kathir attributes the whole chain to Allah's guidance and His will.

Then the other half: "but you cannot make hear those who are in graves." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is stark — just as the dead cannot benefit from guidance and the call to truth after they have died as disbelievers and ended up in the graves, "so too you cannot help these idolators who are decreed to be doomed, and you cannot guide them."

**A precision worth having.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to prevent a misreading, and its care is instructive. Since the passage has already likened disbelievers to the dead and believers to the living, "those in the graves" in this ayah means the disbelievers, "in congruence to this." The sense, it says, is: "the way you cannot make the dead hear you, you can also not make these living disbelievers hear you."

Maʿārif then shows that the ayah itself settles what kind of hearing is being denied. It cannot be hearing in the plain, physical sense: it has "been a matter of common observation that a call was beamed at them, and they did listen to it." What is denied is "the kind of listening that is going to be useful, effective and beneficial" — the listening "because of which the listener forsakes the false and takes to the true." Its illustration: the dead cannot be brought to the right path by being made to hear the Divine Word, because they have "shifted from the avenue of deeds in the world to the arena of recompense in the Hereafter," where even a confession of faith would not be accepted; and the condition of these disbelievers is similar to that.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a careful conclusion: "the present verse has nothing to do with the issue of the ability of the dead to hear. Whether or not the dead hear the living is a different issue in its own place" — and it notes that it has discussed that question in its commentary on Sūrah ar-Rūm and Sūrah an-Naml. That is a habit worth learning from a scholar: an ayah proves what it is about, and being honest about its subject matter is part of respecting it.

## "You are only a warner" (ayah 23)

Ibn Kathir's explanation of "You are only a warner" is short and complete: "all you have to do is to convey the Message and warn them, and Allah leaves astray whomsoever He wills and guides whomsoever He wills."

Two things are stated there side by side, and Ibn Kathir states them without softening either. The Prophet's ﷺ task is naming: convey, and warn. And guidance and misguidance are attributed to Allah's will — He makes whom He wills to hear, He guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills. Ibn Kathir sets both down together, and the believer receives them as he received them, without using one to explain away the other.

Ibn Kathir also shows that being "only a warner" does not mean being only severe, since Allah says immediately after: "Verily, We have sent you with the truth, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner" — which Ibn Kathir explains as "a bearer of glad tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers." Nor is this a lonely role in history. On "And there never was a nation but a warner had passed among them," Ibn Kathir says there was never any nation among the sons of Adam but Allah sent warners to them, "and left them with no excuse." He places beside it "You are only a warner, and to every people there is a guide" (13:7), and "We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger: 'Worship Allah, and avoid all false deities.' Then of them were some whom Allah guided and of them were some upon whom the straying was justified" (16:36).

## Living it

**Stop grading the two parties on worldly terms.** The whole passage is a refusal of false equivalence. Ibn Kathir's road-and-destination reading is the corrective: he asks where each path ends — Gardens with shade and springs, or hot wind and the shadow of black smoke. That is the comparison the ayat are making, and it is not settled by how impressive a path looks at the start.

**Do the work of a warner; leave the outcome to Allah.** If the one sent with revelation was told "all you have to do is to convey the Message and warn them," then no one calling to Allah after him should despair when people do not respond, nor take the credit when they do. And convey the way Ibn Kathir describes the commission: glad tidings as well as warning.

**Ask for the hearing that benefits.** Maʿārif's distinction is not academic. Plenty of people hear the Qur'an recited; the hearing that counts is the kind "because of which the listener forsakes the false and takes to the true." Ibn Kathir attributes that hearing to Allah — which makes it something to ask Him for, not something to assume we already have when we sit down with the Book.

**Live now, while deeds are still the currency.** The reason the dead cannot be made to hear, in Maʿārif's explanation, is that they have shifted from the avenue of deeds into the arena of recompense, where even a confession of faith is no longer accepted. We have not shifted yet. Read that sentence slowly and today's small acts of obedience look exactly as valuable as they are.

passages.title: Every nation received its own warner
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take the pressure off the Prophet ﷺ and put it back where it belongs. He has just been told that he cannot make hearts hear; now he is told what he *was* sent to do, that no nation in history was ever left without someone doing it, and what happened to the peoples who heard such a man and turned away. What holds ayat 24–26 together is a single line of argument: the warner comes, the warner is rejected, the rejecters are seized. Ayah 24 establishes the pattern, ayah 25 places the Prophet's own deniers inside it, ayah 26 shows how the pattern ends.

## The verses just before

A word of context, because ayah 24 answers something. In ayat 19–22 Allah sets out pairs no one would confuse: **"Not alike are the blind and the seeing … Nor are (depths of) darkness and light … Nor are the shade and the sun's heat … Nor are the living and the dead."**

Ibn Kathir explains that these are not idle antonyms. Allah is drawing a parable: the believers are the living, the disbelievers are the dead, and between the blind and the seeing "there is a difference and a huge gap." He reads the whole set as one picture of two destinies. The believer "sees and hears, and walks in the light upon a straight path in this world and the Hereafter, until he comes to settle in Gardens (Paradise) wherein is shade and springs." The disbeliever "is blind and deaf, walking in darkness from which he cannot escape, he is lost in his misguidance in this world and the Hereafter, until he ends up in fierce hot wind and boiling water, and shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor good." Notice that the three earlier pairs reappear in the endings themselves — light and shade for one, darkness and scorching heat for the other. The comparisons were never decoration; they were a map. Ibn Kathir links this to two other places where the Qur'an draws the same contrast: 6:122 (**"Is he who was dead and We gave him life and set for him a light (of belief) whereby he can walk amongst men – like him who is in the (depths of) darkness from which he can never come out?"**) and 11:24 (**"The parable of the two parties is as that of the blind and the deaf and the seer and the hearer. Are they equal when compared?"**).

Then comes the sentence that leads into our passage: **"Verily, Allah makes whom He wills to hear, but you cannot make hear those who are in graves"** (ayah 22). On the first half Ibn Kathir says it means Allah "guides them to listen to the proof and accept it and adhere" to it. On the second half: just as the dead cannot benefit from guidance once they have died as disbelievers, "so too you cannot help these idolators who are decreed to be doomed, and you cannot guide them." Ayah 23 then draws the conclusion — **"You are only a warner"** — which Ibn Kathir glosses: "all you have to do is to convey the Message and warn them, and Allah leaves astray whomsoever He wills and guides whomsoever He wills."

One clarification worth keeping straight before we move on, because the mention of "those who are in graves" is sometimes pulled into a different debate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that since the disbelievers have been likened to the dead and the believers to the living, "those in the graves" here **means the disbelievers**: "the way you cannot make the dead hear you, you can also not make these living disbelievers hear you." And the hearing being denied is a particular kind — "the kind of listening that is going to be useful, effective and beneficial," the listening "because of which the listener forsakes the false and takes to the true." In the plain sense of sound reaching ears they obviously did hear; the commentary notes it has been "a matter of common observation that a call was beamed at them, and they did listen to it." What they did not do was let it change them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore concludes that "the present verse has nothing to do with the issue of the ability of the dead to hear" — a separate question it says is discussed in its commentary on Sūrah ar-Rūm and Sūrah an-Naml.

So the Prophet ﷺ has just been told what he cannot do. Ayah 24 tells him what he can.

## Ayah 24: "We have sent you with the truth"

**"Verily, We have sent you with the truth, a bearer of glad tidings and a warner. And there never was a nation but a warner had passed among them."**

Two things are packed in tightly.

**"A bearer of glad tidings and a warner."** Ibn Kathir gives the pairing its precise targets: "a bearer of glad tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers." Both descriptions are needed, and they land on different people. This also fills out the picture of ayah 23, where the Prophet ﷺ was called *only* a warner. There, the point was the limit of his task — his duty is to convey, while guidance and misguidance rest with Allah. Here the glad tidings stand alongside the warning, so no one imagines the mission is nothing but threat. He carries both; and by Ibn Kathir's own division, which of the two reaches a person depends on which side of the believer–disbeliever line he stands on — the very line ayat 19–22 have just drawn.

**"And there never was a nation but a warner had passed among them."** Ibn Kathir's gloss states both the scope and the consequence: "there was never any nation among the sons of Adam but Allah sent warners to them, and left them with no excuse."

That last phrase is the heart of it. The universality of the warners is not a piece of historical trivia; it is an argument about justice. Nobody arrives at the reckoning able to say they were never told.

Ibn Kathir supports the claim from elsewhere in the Qur'an: **"You are only a warner, and to every people there is a guide"** (13:7), and **"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah, and avoid all false deities.' Then of them were some whom Allah guided and of them were some upon whom the straying was justified"** (16:36). He adds that there are many similar ayat. That second citation is doing double work: it gives the universal sending, and it gives the universal *split* in response. Every nation was warned; in every nation some were guided and some were not. Which is exactly the situation the Prophet ﷺ was living through — and exactly what ayah 25 turns to next.

## Ayah 25: "If they deny you, so did those before them"

**"And if they deny you, those before them also denied. Their Messengers came to them with clear signs, and with the Scriptures, and with the Book giving light."**

Read this as consolation, not as a change of subject. The denial the Prophet ﷺ was meeting is not evidence that something had gone wrong with his mission, and it is not a verdict on him. It is what the peoples before them did to their own messengers. If the warners were universal, so was the rejection.

Then the ayah lists what those earlier messengers arrived carrying, and the list matters because it removes the excuse of insufficient evidence.

- **"With clear signs"** — Ibn Kathir: "clear miracles and definitive proofs." Two kinds of evidence at once: the miracle you witness, and the argument you cannot answer.
- **"And with the Scriptures"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this simply as "the Books." Not only living speech, then, but recorded revelation that outlasts the moment.
- **"And with the Book giving light"** — Ibn Kathir's gloss is "clear and obvious." Nothing in it was murky; nothing needed to be guessed at.

Put the three together and the case is complete. Signs to see, proofs to weigh, Books to keep, and a Book whose message was clear and obvious. Nothing was withheld. So when denial comes anyway, it is not a failure of communication. It is a refusal.

## Ayah 26: "Then I took hold of those who disbelieved"

**"Then I took hold of those who disbelieved, and how terrible was My denial!"**

Ibn Kathir reads the "then" as carrying the full weight of everything listed just before it: "despite all of this, they denied the Messengers and the Message they brought, so I seized them, i.e., with My punishment." The seizing, in other words, is not a mood; it is punishment, and it comes *after* signs, Books and clarity had already been given. This is the same point ayah 24 made from the other end: they were left with no excuse.

**"And how terrible was My denial!"** Ibn Kathir renders the force of it as a question put to the listener: "how great and intense and terrible do you think My punishment was?" That is more devastating than a flat statement would be, because it hands you the work of imagining the answer — and the answer is not something you can fully picture. Ibn Kathir closes the passage with the scholar's reserve: "And Allah knows best."

## Living it

**Deliver, and let go of the outcome.** The single most freeing sentence in this material is Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 23: "all you have to do is to convey the Message and warn them, and Allah leaves astray whomsoever He wills and guides whomsoever He wills." If you have a relative who will not pray, a friend who mocks what you hold sacred, a child who has walked away — your duty is faithfulness in conveying, warmly and clearly. Their heart is not on your ledger. The Prophet ﷺ himself was told this.

**Carry both halves.** He was sent as a bearer of glad tidings *and* a warner — glad tidings to the believers, warning to those who reject. A religion presented as nothing but warning misrepresents the messenger; so does one presented as nothing but reassurance. Part of wisdom is knowing which the particular person in front of you needs to hear.

**Do not read rejection as failure.** Ayah 25 exists so that you stop measuring truth by uptake. Earlier peoples were given clear miracles, definitive proofs, Books, and a message that was clear and obvious — and they still called their messengers liars. If that happened to them, being dismissed is not a sign that you got something wrong.

**And take ayah 26 personally before applying it to anyone else.** Ayah 24 says a warner has passed among every nation, and Ibn Kathir's reason for saying so is that Allah "left them with no excuse." The point of the sequence is not really what those nations did with their warner. It is what we are doing with ours — before the "despite all of this" of ayah 26 is written over us as well.

passages.title: Colours in rain, rock, and flesh: who truly fears Allah
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take a single thing — water falling from the sky — and show how Allah brings out of it an endless variety of colours, then widen the lens to the streaked colours of mountains and the colours of human beings and animals, before turning suddenly inward: **the only people who truly fear Allah are those who know Him.** What holds the passage together is that movement from the visible spectrum of creation to the invisible response it is supposed to produce in a heart. The signs are for everyone to look at; the fear is what happens when someone actually understands what he is looking at.

## Where these ayat sit in the surah

Commentators read the connection in two ways, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports both. Some of the early commentators said the passage returns to the theme of *tawḥīd* — the Oneness of Allah — established through proofs of Allah's power and mastery in nature. Others tied it to what came just before, where the surah had described the different states of people: "And the blind and the sighted are not equal, nor darkness and light, nor shade and the heat of the sun" (35:19–20). On that reading, these two ayat clarify the point further: **mutual difference in Allah's creation is something inherent.** It is there in organic and inorganic substances alike, and not only in shapes and colours but in traits and temperaments too. The variety among human beings the surah has been describing is not an anomaly — it is the same signature that runs through fruit and stone.

## Ayah 27: one water, countless colours

Ibn Kathir's heading for this passage is simply *The Perfect Power of Allah*. His point is precise: Allah is telling us **how He makes different kinds of things out of one thing** — the water He sends down from the heaven. From that single source He brings forth fruits of various colours: yellow, red, green, white and other colours, and with the colours comes an immense variety of tastes and scents as well.

Ibn Kathir brings a parallel ayah to sharpen it:

> "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of vines, and green crops, and date palms growing into two or three from a single stem root, or otherwise, watered with the same water; yet some of them We make more excellent than others to eat. Verily, in these things there are signs for people who understand." (13:4)

Same soil, same rain — different fruit. If the input is uniform and the output is wildly varied, the variety cannot be coming from the water. It is coming from the One who sends it.

## Judad and gharābīb: the words for stone

Then the eye lifts from the orchard to the mountain: *"and among the mountains are judad, white and red, of varying colours, and (others) gharābīb black."*

**Judad.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbās said *al-judad* means **pathways**, and that this was also the view of Abū Mālik, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word's build: *judad* is the plural of *juddah*, whose well-recognised meaning is that of a small pathway, also known as *jādah*. Some respected elders instead took *juddah* in the sense of a tract, patch or segment. Either way — path or patch — the sense lands in the same place: **the parts of a single mountain differ in colour from one another.** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah created the mountains like this, with different colours, and that we do indeed see white mountains and red ones, and that in some of them there are streaks which are themselves of varying colours. So the sign is not only that mountain differs from mountain, but that one mountain is banded within itself.

**Gharābīb.** Ibn Kathir adds that there are some mountains which are very black. ʿIkrimah said *al-gharābīb* means mountains that are **high and black**, and this was also the view of Abū Mālik, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī and Qatādah. Ibn Jarīr adds the linguistic note that carries the flavour of the word: **when the Arabs describe something as being very black, they say *ghirbīb*.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the ordering. **White is mentioned first, black last**, and in between — alongside the mention of red — comes the expression *mukhtalifun alwānuhā*, "of different colours." This could be releasing a hint, it suggests: that in reality the colours in this world are no more than two, white and black, and the rest of the colours in the spectrum emerge by compounding different degrees of white and black.

## A subtle grammatical point

Here is a detail that only opens up in the Arabic, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes much of it.

The Qur'an mentions the differing colours of **fruits** in ayah 27, and then the differing colours of **mountains** — but the grammatical style is different in the two places. With regard to the fruits, the difference of colour is expressed by an **adverbial phrase**. In the case of the mountains, it is expressed by an **adjectival phrase**.

According to Arabic grammar, an adjective normally refers to a **permanent** quality of a thing, whereas an adverb may refer to a quality or condition that is **subject to change**. Keeping this in view, there may be a hint here: the difference of colour in fruits **does not remain constant in a single state** — it keeps changing after brief intervals, as anyone who has watched fruit ripen knows. The colours of human beings and other life forms are, by contrast, generally fast and abiding; they do not change.

## Ayah 28: the same signature in flesh

*"And likewise, men and moving creatures and cattle are of various colours."*

Ibn Kathir explains that the same is true of living creatures too: humans and animals — all creatures which walk on their feet — and cattle. He points out a rhetorical move in the wording: **here something general is followed by something specific.** *Ad-dawābb* covers moving creatures broadly; *al-anʿām*, cattle, is then named specifically from within that broader category.

On the colours of people, Ibn Kathir gives concrete examples from the world as he knew it: among mankind there are Berbers, Ethiopians and some non-Arabs who are very black, and Slavs and Romans who are very white, and the Arabs, who are in between, and the Indians. And he cites the parallel from Sūrat ar-Rūm:

> "...and the difference of your languages and colours. Verily, in that are indeed signs for men of sound knowledge." (30:22)

The Qur'an treats the range of human complexion the way it treats the streaks in a mountain and the colours of ripening fruit — as **evidence**, not as hierarchy. Similarly, Ibn Kathir adds, animals and cattle vary in their colours, even within one species, and a single animal may have patches of different colours. His response to all of it is a phrase of praise: *Blessed be Allah, the Best of creators.*

## The hinge: where does *kadhālika* belong?

Ayah 28 contains the word *kadhālika* ("likewise" / "similarly"), and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a genuine question about it: does it close the sentence before it, or open the sentence after it?

According to the **consensus of the majority** of commentators and scholars, this is a place of *waqf* — a stop in recitation. On that reading *kadhālika* is related to the previous subject, and the sense is that the creation of all that exists in categories and kinds and different colours is a very special sign of the power and wisdom of Allah.

But there are also narrations suggesting that the word is related to the sentence that **follows**. If that interpretation is adopted, the stop comes earlier, after "having different colours," and *kadhālika* is translated "similarly" — meaning: *the way fruits, mountains, human beings and other life forms are marked out by different colours, similarly there are different degrees among people who have the awe or fear of Allah in their hearts.* Someone may have achieved its highest degree; others may have arrived at what is less than that. And the whole thing depends on knowledge: **whoever has a certain degree of knowledge will have a corresponding degree of the awe or fear of Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this reading to *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*.

On that second reading the passage folds back on itself: the spectrum of colours in the world becomes a picture of the spectrum of *khashyah* — reverent fear — in the hearts of those who look at it.

## "It is only those who have knowledge among His servants that fear Allah"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a symmetry with an earlier ayah in the surah: "You only warn those who fear their Lord unseen" (35:18), which was consolation for the Prophet ﷺ — meaning that when he warns people and conveys the message of Allah to them, only those who have the awe of Allah without having seen Him get the maximum benefit out of it. In symmetry with that, this ayah mentions people of whom it can be said that they have the awe of Allah and fear Him as is His due. There is a further parallelism: where the earlier passages mentioned the disbelievers and deniers along with the different states they were submerged in, this ayah puts forth the opposite — it speaks particularly of the men of Allah, His *awliyāʼ*.

**Why knowledge produces fear.** Ibn Kathir's explanation is the heart of it: only those who have knowledge truly fear Him **as He should be feared** — because the more they know about the Almighty, the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, who has the most perfect attributes and is described with the most beautiful Names, the more they will fear Him. Fear here is not superstition; it is the natural weight that settles on a heart the moment it grasps something true about who Allah is.

**What *innamā* is doing.** The verse opens with *innamā*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles the grammar carefully. *Innamā* is used in Arabic to describe *ḥaṣr* — exclusiveness — so the sentence obviously means that **only** the *ʿulamāʼ*, the knowing and the learned, fear Allah with genuine awe. But the tafsir authority **Ibn ʿAṭiyyah** and others said that *innamā*, besides being employed to show exclusiveness, is also used to describe **the singularity of something** — and the latter is what is meant here: that fearing Allah and remaining in awe of Him is an attribute **specially incumbent on the *ʿulamāʼ*.** It does not necessarily imply that those other than them have no such fear and awe in them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this to *al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ* of Abū Ḥayyān.

### Who, then, counts as one of the *ʿulamāʼ*?

The *ʿulamāʼ* in this ayah, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, means **people who have due knowledge of the being and attributes of Allah**, and who have the fact of His power and control, and His favours and blessings upon what He has created, always in sight. In the terminology of the Qur'an, **no one is considered to be an *ʿālim* simply by virtue of knowing the Arabic language, grammar and rhetoric**, unless he has acquired the knowledge and understanding of the attributes of Allah in that manner.

Ibn Kathir gathers the early voices:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah) said they are **those who know that Allah is able to do all things.** He also said: the one among His servants who knows about ar-Raḥmān is the one who **does not associate anything in worship with Him; who accepts as lawful what He has permitted and as unlawful what He has prohibited; who obeys His commands; and who is certain that he will meet Him and be brought to account for his deeds.**
- **Saʿīd bin Jubayr**: "**Fear is what stands between you and disobeying Allah**, may He be glorified."
- **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: the knowledgeable person is the one who **fears ar-Raḥmān with regard to the Unseen, who likes that which Allah wants him to like, and who shuns that which angers Allah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports his words as: an *ʿālim* is one who **fears Allah in private and in public**, likes what Allah likes him to do, and hates what is detestable in the sight of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds several more:

- **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd** said that memorising many aḥādīth — or simply talking a lot — is not *ʿilm*; real knowledge comes when one has the awe and fear of Allah along with it. In short, the degree of the fear of Allah a person has is the degree to which he is an *ʿālim*.
- **Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Miṣrī** (cited via Ibn Kathir): fear of Allah cannot be recognised on the basis of someone's prolific reporting of events or abundance of knowledge; it is identified through **his adherence to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Prophet.**
- **Shaykh Shahābuddīn as-Suhrawardī** said this ayah clearly indicates that **a person who has no fear of Allah is no *ʿālim*** (cited from *Mazharī*) — and this is confirmed by the sayings of the Salaf, the early forbears of Islam. **Rabīʿ ibn Anas**: "One who does not fear Allah is not an *ʿālim*." **Mujāhid**: "Only he who fears Allah is the real *ʿālim*."
- When **Saʿd ibn Ibrāhīm** was asked who in the city of Madinah knew the Divine Law best, he answered: **he who is the most fearing of his Lord.**

**ʿAlī ؓ on what a real jurist is.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites through Qurṭubī his definition of a *faqīh* — a master of Islamic jurisprudence — as one who **would not make people lose hope in the mercy of Allah, nor leave them free to indulge in acts of disobedience to Him, nor give them the guarantee of remaining safe from the punishment of Allah, nor forsake the Qur'an by indulging in pursuits other than it.** And he said: there is no good in an act of worship that is without knowledge, no good in knowledge that is without understanding, and no recitation without deliberation in it. Look at the balance in that: a scholar who only frightens people has failed, and so has a scholar who only reassures them.

### Three kinds of knowledgeable person

Ibn Kathir preserves a saying narrated by Sufyān ath-Thawrī from Abū Ḥayyān at-Taymī, from a man, that it used to be said the knowledgeable are of three types:

1. **One who knows Allah and knows the command of Allah** — he is the one who fears Allah and knows the limits (*ḥudūd*) and the obligatory duties (*farāʼiḍ*).
2. **One who knows Allah but does not know the command of Allah** — he fears Allah but does not know the limits and the obligatory duties.
3. **One who knows the command of Allah but does not know Allah** — he knows the limits and the obligatory duties but **does not fear Allah**.

The ayah's logic is then unmistakable: information about the law is one thing, knowledge of the Lawgiver another. Only the first type has both.

### Two degrees of the fear of Allah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*) closes with a distinction that keeps this from becoming crushing. At times awe and fear of Allah are rooted in a person's **creed and reason**, because of which he adheres to the injunctions of the Sharīʿah as a matter of obligation. And there are occasions when this awe and fear become **the very state of one's existence**, rising to the degree of a firmly ingrained asset whereby readiness to follow the Sharīʿah becomes a natural reflex. **The first degree is mandatory, and for an *ʿālim* necessary. The second is certainly superior and sublime — but not necessary.**

The same source notes that the clarifications above also help remove a doubt many people feel: what about the many *ʿulamāʼ* who do not seem to have the kind of awe and fear of Allah required of them? The answer the passage gives is not to lower the standard but to correct the label — in the sight of Allah, bland knowledge of Arabic is not what *ʿilm* is, and the one who is merely proficient in it is not an *ʿālim*. **Anyone who does not have the fear of Allah in his heart is simply not an *ʿālim* in the terminology of the Qur'an.**

## "Verily, Allah is Almighty, Oft-Forgiving"

The passage ends on two Names held together — *ʿAzīz*, the Almighty, and *Ghafūr*, the Oft-Forgiving. Ibn Kathir's explanation of fear rests on exactly this: the more a servant knows of the Almighty, the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, who has the most perfect attributes and the most beautiful Names, the more he will fear Him. And the ayah itself pairs the Names: the One to be feared is also the One who forgives. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, having given his definition of the knowledgeable person, recited the ayah through to this very ending — so the fear it calls for is never fear cut off from hope.

## Living it

**Test knowledge by its effect, not its volume.** The ayah does not ask how much you have memorised; the Salaf quoted above ask whether it has changed what you love, what you avoid, and how you behave when nobody is watching.

**Use Saʿīd bin Jubayr's measure.** If what you call fear of Allah does not actually stand between you and a sin you are about to commit, it has not yet become fear in the sense the ayah means.

**Let the study of creation be study of Allah.** Rain, ripening fruit, banded rock, the range of human faces — ayat 27 and 28 treat all of it as evidence. Looking at the world attentively is not a distraction from knowing Allah; according to these ayat it is one of the routes to it — and ayah 28 puts the variety of human complexions in that same list, as signs of one Creator's power, not grounds for ranking anyone.

passages.title: The trade that never fails
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat describe the people of true knowledge from the inside out — and then price their deeds as a business deal. Ayah 29 lists three visible habits of the believing servant (reciting Allah's Book, establishing the prayer, spending from what Allah has provided) and calls the whole enterprise "a trade that will never perish." Ayah 30 completes the thought by telling us what the returns look like: wages paid in full, then an increase out of pure grace. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the two are grammatically linked — *liyuwaffiyahum* ("so that He pays them in full") in ayah 30 is connected with *lan tabūra* ("that never fails") in ayah 29 — so the trade that never fails is defined by the payout that follows.

## Where this comes from in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the passage just before this, ayah 28, described the true ʿulamāʾ — those who truly acknowledge Allah — by a quality of the **heart**: the awe of Allah within it. Ayah 29 now turns to the same blessed people, whom the commentary calls "the *awliyāʾ* or men of Allah," and mentions qualities of theirs that "find expression through outward parts of the body." So this is not a new subject; it is the visible half of a picture whose invisible half was awe. Inward reverence, if it is real, comes out through the tongue, the limbs and the wallet.

## Three marks that show on the outside

**1. They recite the Book of Allah.** The Arabic verb is *yatlūna*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to its form — the *muḍāriʿ*, which the commentary calls the "aorist" tense, the Arabic form used for ongoing, repeated action rather than a single completed act. The commentary says this wording "releases a hint" that these are people who recite the Book of Allah **constantly** — recitation is a settled habit of their lives, not an occasional visit to the text.

There is a genuine difference among the commentators here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that other elders took *yatlūna* in its literal sense of *following* — that is, they *follow* the Qur'an in deed. The commentary judges the first reading (actual recitation) to be the weightier one, noting that the word *tilāwah* (recitation) is used here in its recognised sense. But it immediately adds the point that keeps this from becoming a technicality: it "stands determined from the context" that recitation can be trustworthy only when it brings forth actions in accordance with the Qur'an. So both readings end up in the same place. Recitation is meant, and recitation that produces nothing is not what is being praised.

Ibn Kathir puts a similar balance in different words: these are believing servants "who recite **and believe in** His Book, and do the deeds prescribed in it."

On the strength of this ayah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes **Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Shikhkhīr** (may Allah have mercy on him), who said: *hādhihi āyat al-qurrāʾ* — "This verse is for al-qurrāʾ," meaning those who make the recitation of the Qur'an the special activity of their lives.

**2. They establish the prayer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this as the second quality, and elsewhere describes it as establishing salah "as due." Ibn Kathir specifies what that involves: performing "regular prayer at the prescribed times, night and day."

**3. They spend from what Allah has provided.** Ibn Kathir glosses this as "spending (in charity) out of that which Allah has provided for them, secretly and openly." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this third quality as the spending of their wealth in the way of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes an observation about the three together: from people who carry these qualities — reciting the Qur'an constantly, establishing salah as due, and spending in the way of Allah cheerfully — "it is also expected that they would not simply stop at Fard and Wajib spending, rather, would also be contributing to voluntary charities." The three habits together generate a generosity that goes past the minimum.

## "Secretly and openly"

The ayah says they spend *sirran wa ʿalāniyah* — secretly and openly. Both commentaries treat this as deliberate guidance, not decoration.

The first thing it indicates, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that **it is often better to spend secretly**, in order to stay safe from *riyāʾ* — showing off in acts of worship, doing the deed so that others see it.

But "openly" is in the ayah too, and the commentary notes that religious considerations sometimes require it. It gives two illustrations: congregational prayer, "for which the command is to call adhan from minarets and perform salah openly with the highest possible attendance"; and occasions where it is necessary that spending in the way of Allah be open, in order to persuade others to do the same.

Muslim jurists, it continues, have laid out the details for both prayer and spending:

- Where the act is **farḍ** (obligatory), **wājib** (necessary), or **sunnah muʾakkadah** (emphasised sunnah), doing it **openly** is better.
- Other than this — as with *nafl* (voluntary) prayer — it is better to do it **privately**.
- In wealth: where spending is farḍ or wājib, such as the obligatory **Zakāh**, **ṣadaqat al-fiṭr**, or **qurbānī**, spending openly is better and worthy of more merit.
- As for the rest — voluntary charity (*ṣadaqah nāfilah*) — spending secretly **carries more merit and grace**.

## Why "trade"?

Then comes the phrase that names the passage: *yarjūna tijāratan lan tabūra* — "they hope for a trade that will never perish."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *lan tabūra* as a derivation from **بَوَار (bawār)**, which means *to go waste*. The verse means, it says, that believers with these attributes "hope to go in a trade that never runs into a loss."

Why frame worship as commerce at all? Because, the commentary explains, "a trader invests his capital and time in some venture only when he hopes that by doing so, his capital will increase and he will profit by it." And the Qur'an uses this same image elsewhere: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Sūrah aṣ-Ṣaff, *"O those who believe, shall I tell you about a trade that saves you from a painful punishment? (It is that) you believe in Allah and His Messenger, and carry out Jihad in His way with your riches and your lives"* (61:10).

Then comes the turn. **Every trading activity in this world, the commentary says, is hemmed with the probability of loss along with the hope of profit.** By adding *lan tabūra* to *tijārah*, it was pointed out that in this deal — the one made for the sake of the benefits of the Hereafter — "there was no probability of a loss." And so, in the commentary's words, the good people of Allah who take pains to do what is good and right "do not go about running a business as businesses are commonly run"; instead they hope to engage in a trading activity that never suffers a loss.

## "They hope" — the humility built into the wording

The ayah does not say they *know* their reward is secured; it says *yarjūna*, **they hope**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing *Rūḥ ul Maʿānī*) treats this single word as one of the most important things in the passage.

Its point: the word *yarjūna* indicates that a believer has no room for certainty in any good deed done in this mortal world. No one can say it will definitely bring forgiveness and that the reward is assured. Three reasons are given:

1. **The debt is unpayable.** No matter how good one is in deeds, one simply cannot fulfil the right of reverence and worship that Allah Taʿālā has over His servants. Therefore forgiveness for one and all will not be possible without the grace of Allah — a point the commentary says has been clearly stated in a hadith. (The commentary does not name a collection here, so neither will we; the teaching stands as it reports it.)
2. **The deed can be contaminated.** Even while doing everything good, one should not neglect the danger of "some secret trick of Satan or one's own self" getting mixed up with the good deeds, because of which they do not remain acceptable.
3. **A deed can be blocked by another.** On occasions, along with a good deed some bad deed gets committed, which in turn stops the good deed from being accepted.

Hence the conclusion: even after having become particular with all possible good deeds, no one has the right to become sure of his or her salvation and of the high ranks that follow in its wake. **The most one can do is hope.** That is not gloom — it is the posture the ayah places in the mouths of the very best of people.

And notice the tenderness the commentary finds in it. That these people are described by their *hope* "serves as a delicate hint" that Allah Taʿālā is the noblest of the noble and the most generous of the generous — and so **He will not sever the hope of the hopeful; instead He would fulfil it.**

## Ayah 30: paid in full, then more

*"So that He pays them their rewards in full, and gives them more out of His grace."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the grammatical link already mentioned: *liyuwaffiyahum* ("so that He pays them in full") is connected with *lan tabūra* ("has no loss"). That is the engine of the passage — this trade of theirs not only admits of no loss, "but that it will also bring their return and reward in full, and in addition to that, Allah Taʿālā will bless them, out of His grace, with much more."

There is a beautiful asymmetry here, and the commentary states it plainly: their hope was limited to receiving only a full return on their deed, but Allah Taʿālā would, in His infinite mercy, bestow on them much more — "far beyond their fondest hopes of returns." Ibn Kathir says something similar: He gives them a reward for what they have done, "and multiply it by adding more, such as has never occurred to them." The increase is not merely a larger version of what they imagined; it is outside what they imagined.

What is inside this "increase out of His grace"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names three things:

**The multiplication of reward.** Included within this grace is Allah's promise that He rewards the deed of a believer multiplied many times — "the lowest denominator of which could be ten times of the deed, and the highest could reach seven hundred times, even higher than that."

**The acceptance of their intercession for sinners.** Here the commentary reports a hadith narrated by Sayyidnā **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd** (may Allah be pleased with him), in which he reported the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of this grace: *"These people will intercede on behalf of anyone who had done some favor to them during the life of the mortal world. Then, despite being deserving of the punishment of Jahannam, such people will stand delivered of it by virtue of their intercession."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this as **Tafsīr Mazharī with reference to Ibn Abī Ḥātim**. The commentary adds the obvious qualification: intercession will be possible only for the people of faith — no one will be allowed to intercede on behalf of a disbeliever.

**Seeing Allah.** The foremost part of this grace, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that they will have an opportunity to see Allah Taʿālā.

## "Indeed He is Ghafūr, Shakūr"

The ayah closes on two of Allah's names, and Ibn Kathir gives each a single clean gloss:

- **Ghafūr** — Oft-Forgiving: "He forgives their sins."
- **Shakūr** — Most Ready to appreciate: "He appreciates even a little of their good deeds."

Take the two together and you have both sides of the ledger of this trade named in one breath: the sins are forgiven, and even a little of the good is appreciated. It is worth pausing on the second, because it is startling to read that Allah describes Himself as Most Ready to appreciate — and worth taking it in exactly the sense Ibn Kathir gives it, no more and no less: even the little you manage is not overlooked.

## Living it

The passage hands you a short, unglamorous list, and it is worth reading as a checklist rather than a poem:

- **Recitation as a habit, not an event.** The tense of *yatlūna* asks for constancy. A daily portion you actually keep is closer to this ayah than an ambitious plan you abandon — and the commentators insist that recitation is trustworthy only when it brings forth action in accordance with the Qur'an.
- **Prayer at its times.** Ibn Kathir's gloss puts the emphasis on the prescribed times, night and day.
- **Give, and think about who is watching.** For Zakāh and the obligatory dues, open is better. For voluntary giving, secret carries more merit — and the reason the commentary gives is protection: it keeps *riyāʾ* out of the deed.
- **Hope, but do not audit yourself into certainty.** The best people in this ayah are described as *hoping*. Keep working; keep the outcome in Allah's hands — and remember the delicate hint, that He does not sever the hope of the hopeful.
- **Trust the terms of the deal.** This is the one venture with no probability of loss — and the payout, the commentary says, runs far beyond your fondest hopes of returns.

passages.title: Heirs of the Book and the Home of everlasting settlement
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat trace one line: Allah revealed the Book to His Prophet ﷺ as the truth (ayah 31), then handed it down as an *inheritance* to a community He Himself chose (ayah 32), and then shows where the inheritance ends: the Gardens of eternity, the adornment, and the words the heirs speak as they walk in (ayat 33–35).

## Ayah 31 — the Book that is the truth

Ibn Kathir reads the address as personal: *O Muhammad* — "what We have revealed to you of the Book" is the Qur'an. The word **muṣaddiqan** ("confirming") points two ways at once. The Qur'an confirms the earlier Books, and it confirms them, as Ibn Kathir says, "just as they bore witness to the coming of the Qur'an and that it would be sent down from the Lord of the worlds."

Two of Allah's names then close the ayah: **"Verily Allah is indeed All-Aware (Khabīr) and All-Seer (Baṣīr) of His servants."** Ibn Kathir answers that this concerns how Allah distributes His gifts: "He is All-Aware of them and knows who deserves to receive the blessing which He may give to him and not to others." Hence, he adds, the Prophets and the Messengers are favoured above the rest of mankind, some Prophets given more than others and higher status than others — and the position given to Muhammad ﷺ is higher than that of all of them, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all.

## Ayah 32 — "Then We gave the Book as an inheritance"

**"Then" (thumma).** Grammatically, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, *thumma* joins back to **"We revealed" (awḥaynā)** in ayah 31, and signals precedence and succession — sometimes in time, sometimes in rank. Both fit. The Qur'an's descent upon the Prophet ﷺ through revelation comes first in rank and degree; its bestowal on his community comes after. And read in the light of the ḥadīth that Prophets do not leave coins of gold and silver as inheritance but leave knowledge as their legacy, it is a sequence in time too: *We blessed you with this Book; then you passed it on to your community as its inheritor.*

**"We gave as inheritance" (awrathnā).** To make someone inherit, notes Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is to bestow, to give as legacy or gift — and the choice of *inheritance* makes a precise point: exactly as an heir receives his share without having done anything to acquire it, this wealth of the noble Qur'an has been given as a gift to these chosen servants without any effort of their own. You woke up owning it.

**"Those We have chosen" (alladhīna iṣṭafaynā).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that **iṣṭifāʼ** — to choose, to pick out — is the Qur'an's vocabulary for Prophets and angels: "Allah chooses messengers from the angels and from men" (al-Ḥajj 22:75); "Verily Allah has chosen Adam and Nūḥ and the House of Ibrāhīm and the House of ʿImrān over the worlds" (Āl ʿImrān 3:33). Here Allah places the Muslim ummah in line with those chosen ones — though, it carefully adds, the degrees of that choice vary: the choosing of Prophets and angels occupies a higher degree.

Ibn Kathir: "They are this Ummah." ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbās — the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, whom Allah caused to inherit *every* Book He had revealed; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why that is no exaggeration: the Qur'an, being the Book that confirms and preserves all previous Scriptures, encompasses their contents, so to inherit it is to inherit them all. On the view of the majority of commentators the phrase means this Ummah — its scholars directly, and everyone else through them.

## The three kinds of heir

Ibn Kathir defines them:

- **"Some who wrong themselves" (ẓālim li-nafsihi)** — those who are careless about doing some obligatory actions, and who commit some forbidden actions.
- **"Some who follow a middle course" (muqtaṣid)** — those who fulfil their obligations and avoid things that are forbidden, but who may neglect some good deeds and do some things which are disliked.
- **"Some who are, by Allah's leave, foremost in good deeds" (sābiq bi'l-khayrāt)** — those who do the obligatory *and* the encouraged, avoid the unlawful *and* the disliked, and avoid even some actions which are permissible; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, out of devotion to acts of worship or because of some doubt about a thing's lawfulness.

Notice that **"by Allah's leave"** is attached only to the third group: racing ahead in good is itself something granted. Muhammad Ibn al-Bāqir defined the first kind simply as "a person who mixes good and bad deeds." And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests why the order runs from worst to best: perhaps because those unjust to themselves are the largest number, those of the middle course fewer, and those ahead in good deeds fewer still.

Ibn ʿAbbās gave the three outcomes in one breath: **"those who wrong themselves will be forgiven, those who follow a middle course will have an easy accounting, and those who are foremost in good deeds will enter Paradise without being brought to account."** In another report from him: those of the middle course enter Paradise by the mercy of Allah, and those who wronged themselves — together with the Aṣḥāb al-Aʿrāf — by the intercession of Muhammad ﷺ. Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said one day: **"My intercession will be for those among my Ummah who commit major sins."**

## Are the wrongdoers really among "the chosen"?

Ibn Kathir reports the disagreement plainly: it was reported from a number of the Salaf that those of this Ummah who wrong themselves are *still* among those whom Allah has chosen; others said the wrongdoers are not part of this Ummah at all, not among those Allah chose and not among the inheritors of the Book. Ibn Kathir's verdict: **"The correct view is that they are also part of this Ummah."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees, holding it already proved from many authentic aḥādīth that each of the three kinds belongs to the Muslim ummah and none is excluded from *"whom We chose"* — and calls it the ultimate merit of this ummah's believing servants that even those somewhat wanting in deeds share in this supreme distinction.

**The scene behind one report.** Ibn Jarīr reports from Abū Thābit that he went to the mosque one of those days, found Abū ad-Dardāʼ already sitting there, sat down by his side and began to pray: *"O Allah, mollify the loneliness and anxiety of my heart, and have mercy on me in my state of homelessness, and make it easy on me by sending a good companion."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over that: the early forbears of Islam placed great emphasis on the quest for a good companion, treating it as an important objective in life. Hearing the prayer, Abū ad-Dardāʼ said: "If you are honest in your prayer, then I am more fortunate than you" — Allah had blessed him with a good companion on the spot, without his asking. Then: I will relate to you a ḥadīth I heard from the Prophet ﷺ. He mentioned this very ayah, and said that those who race ahead of others in good deeds will go to Paradise without reckoning; those in the middle will face an accounting that will be easy on them; and the unjust, the ones who fall short in deeds and are prone to slip into sins, **will be overwhelmed with remorse at that juncture — and after that they too will be asked to enter Paradise, and all their sorrows will stand removed from them.**

Among the narrations Ibn Kathir gathered here is one from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, that the Prophet ﷺ said of these three kinds, **"They rank alike and alike they are in Jannah, all of them"** — where "being in one rank," Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means that all of them will be forgiven and all will go to Paradise, not that there is no variance between their ranks.

**ʿĀ'ishah's answer.** Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī reports that ʿUqbah Ibn Ṣahbān Hanāʼī asked ʿĀ'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, about this ayah. She said: "My son, all these three kinds are to go to Paradise. Out of these, those who were ahead of everyone in good deeds were people who passed away during the period of the Holy Prophet ﷺ — he himself testified that they are to go to Jannah. And those who took the middle course are people who followed the former as their role models to the extent that they joined up with them. **As for those who have been unjust to themselves, they are people like me and you!**" Certainly great was her modesty, observes Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — she counted herself in the third kind, although according to clear statements in sound and authentic aḥādīth she ranks high among *as-sābiqūn al-awwalūn*, the very first and foremost people of early Islam.

## The scholars: heirs of the heirs

Ibn Kathir writes that the scholars are the most fortunate of people with regard to this blessing, and the most entitled to this mercy; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees that the ʿulamāʼ are the direct inheritors of the knowledge relating to the Book of Allah and of the mission of the Prophets.

Ibn Kathir supports it with the report Imam Ahmad recorded from Qays bin Kathīr: one of the people of Madīnah came to Abū ad-Dardāʼ when he was in Damascus and said he had come only to seek one ḥadīth he had heard Abū ad-Dardāʼ narrate. Abū ad-Dardāʼ then said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

> "Whoever follows a path to seek knowledge, Allah will show him the way to Paradise. The angels lower their wings being pleased with the one who seeks knowledge. Whoever is in the heavens and on earth, even the fish in the sea, ask for forgiveness for the scholar. The superiority of the scholar over the worshipper is like that of the moon over all other heavenly bodies. The scholars are the heirs of the Prophets, for the Prophets did not leave behind Dinars and Dirhams, but they left behind knowledge; and whoever receives it, receives an abundance of good fortune."

Ibn Kathir notes it was also reported by Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration from Thaʿlabah Ibn al-Ḥakam that Allah will address the ʿulamāʼ of this community on the Day of Judgment and say: *"I had placed My knowledge and wisdom in your chests, for I had intended to forgive you irrespective of the nature of your actual deeds"* (reported also by aṭ-Ṭabarānī, with all the chains of authority he cites described as reliable — Tafsīr Mazharī). But it guards this against misuse: it is already established from the earlier presentation (the quality of the true ʿulamāʼ in ayah 28) that a person who has no awe and fear of Allah is simply not counted as one of the ʿulamāʼ. So the address is to people for whom awe of Allah has become their natural reflex, making it virtually impossible for them to indulge in sins carelessly — though on occasions even they may slip, and it is that slip the forgiveness covers.

## Ayah 33 — "That is the great favour": the Gardens of ʿAdn

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the join carefully. When ayah 32 ends, **"That — that is indeed a great grace,"** the *that* is the counting of all three of these kinds among His chosen servants.

On the adornment, Ibn Kathir cites what was recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"The ornaments of the believer will reach as far as his wuḍūʼ."** The jewellery of Paradise follows the line the water traced in this world.

On the silk, it is forbidden to men here precisely because it is theirs there. Ibn Kathir cites what was recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, **"Whoever wears silk in this world, will not wear it in the Hereafter,"** and, from the same source, **"It is for them in this world, and for you in the Hereafter."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the fuller narration — Ḥudhayfah heard the Prophet ﷺ saying, "Do not wear dresses of silk and do not drink water in utensils of gold and silver, nor use plates made of these in eating food — because these things are for disbelievers in this world and for you, in the Hereafter" (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) — along with a report from ʿUmar to the same effect (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), and a narration of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that a man who wears silk in this world will remain deprived of it in the Hereafter, *even if he were to go to Paradise* (Mazharī).

To the objection that ornaments are for women and do not suit men, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān replies bluntly that taking the conditions of the Hereafter on the analogy of the conditions of this mortal world is unreasonable. And Imam al-Qurṭubī harmonises the verses: commentators explain that every inhabitant of Paradise will have bracelets to wear of gold, silver *and* pearls — which is why one verse mentions "of silver" (76:21) and others "of gold" (18:31; 22:23; 35:33; 43:53).

## Ayah 34 — "Praise be to Allah, who has removed our grief"

What is **al-ḥazan**? Ibn Kathir: it means "fear of everything that is feared; it has been lifted from us and we have been relieved of all that we used to fear of the anxieties of the world and the Hereafter." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says leading commentators gave various explanations, but the truth of the matter is that all sorrows are included — and it names four: the concerns of this life; the concern of the Day of Judgment and Resurrection; the concern of the Reckoning of Deeds; and the concern of the punishment of Hellfire.

On the first of the four it is unsentimental: in this world one may become a king or a prophet or a saint and still not escape sorrow, which is why the people of wisdom call this world a home of sorrows, and why it quotes the Persian line, *In this world no one is free of sorrow — and if one is, one is not a human being.* Imam Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ said much the same: it is the typical state of a believer that he never remains free of concerns while in this world — the Prophet ﷺ said that the world is a prison for the believer — which is why the accounts of the lives of the Prophet ﷺ and his great Companions show these blessed souls looking sad fairly often. Sadness here is not proof that something has gone wrong with your faith. It is the address you live at, and ayah 34 is the day you move out.

**"Our Lord is indeed Oft-Forgiving (Ghafūr), Most Ready to appreciate (Shakūr)."** Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained the pairing beautifully: **"He forgives them for their major sins, and appreciates even the smallest of their good deeds."**

There is also a narration from ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said that for the people who uphold the kalimah *lā ilāha illā Allāh* there is no fear or loneliness at the time of death, nor in the grave, nor when they rise again on the Day of Resurrection — "as if I am virtually seeing them rise from their respective graves saying: *Praise be to Allah who has removed all sorrow from us*" (reported by aṭ-Ṭabarānī, Mazharī). So whose sentence is it — the wrongdoers' or every believer's? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles them: it is a statement that will be made by all the people of Paradise, whichever of the three kinds they belong to, but the one who wronged himself carries an additional and more serious sorrow on the plains of the Resurrection, which is removed at the moment of his entry. The thought that each one's roster of sorrows is his own, it adds, is not too far out.

## Ayah 35 — the Home of settlement, given as pure grace

**"Who, out of His grace, has settled us in the Home of everlasting settlement (dār al-muqāmah)."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws three characteristics of that home from the ayah: it is an eternal home, with no danger of any lapse of time or of expulsion from it; no one there will face any sorrow; and no one there will experience the least fatigue or boredom.

Then **min faḍlihi**, "out of His grace." Ibn Kathir spells out what the people of Paradise mean by it: *Who has given us this position and status out of His grace and blessing and mercy, for our good deeds are not equivalent to this.* And he cites what was reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"None of you will enter Paradise by virtue of his good deeds."** They said, "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: **"Not even me, unless Allah encompasses me with His mercy and grace."**

**"No toil will touch us there, nor will weariness touch us."** Ibn Kathir notes that **naṣab** and **lughūb** both mean exhaustion, and suggests that negating both may mean that neither their bodies nor their souls will become exhausted; *and Allah knows best.* Their obligations come to an end when they enter Paradise, where they will enjoy eternal rest and repose — "Eat and drink at ease for that which you have sent on before you in days past" (69:24).

## Living it

- Ibn Kathir's definitions are concrete enough to measure yourself against: are the obligations kept and the forbidden avoided? Are the encouraged and the disliked taken seriously at all?
- If you are in the first group, the door is not shut. But read Abū ad-Dardāʼ's ḥadīth honestly: that group reaches the Resurrection overwhelmed with remorse first. Forgiveness is not the same as an easy journey.
- Ayah 35 forbids you from ever adding up your deeds and presenting the bill — "our good deeds are not equivalent to this." Not even the Prophet ﷺ enters except by Allah's mercy and grace. So work like an heir who owes everything to the one who left it, and lean at the end on **min faḍlihi** — *out of His grace* — which is the phrase the heirs themselves are given to say.

passages.title: The disbelievers screaming in the Fire
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat turn the page from Paradise to the Fire: having just described the home of the blessed, Allah now shows us the condition of those who rejected Him — a punishment that never kills and never eases, a desperate plea to be sent back for a second chance, and Allah's answer to that plea. What holds the passage together is a single argument: the excuse has already been used up. Ayah 36 shows the sentence, ayah 37 shows the appeal and its refusal, and ayah 38 closes the case by naming the One who judges it — the Knower of every hidden thing, including what is inside a chest.

## The turn from Paradise to the Fire

Ibn Kathir marks the hinge plainly: "Having told us how the blessed will be (in Paradise), Allah now starts to tell us what the state of doomed will be."

That contrast is worth holding in mind, because the immediately preceding ayah had the people of Paradise praising Allah for a home where "neither we are touched by weariness. Nor are we touched by boredom." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out three features of that home: it is eternal, with no danger of any lapse of time or of expulsion from it; no one there will face any sorrow; and no one there will experience the least fatigue or boredom — unlike this mortal world, where one needs to sleep after work.

Read ayah 36 straight after that, and every feature is inverted. Their home is also permanent — Ibn Kathir cites "Verily, the criminals will be in the torment of Hell to abide therein forever" (43:74) and the keeper's answer, "Verily, you shall abide forever" (43:77) — but it is the Fire. Their condition also never changes, but it never eases. And the rest that a body craves after labour never arrives: as Ibn Kathir puts it, they will think that if only they could die it would be a time of rest for them, but that can never happen to them.

## Ayah 36: a punishment that will not finish them

**"Neither will it have a complete killing effect on them so that they die."** Ibn Kathir puts this beside another ayah about the wretched in the Fire: "Wherein he will neither die nor live" (20:74) — a state suspended between the two.

He also cites what was reported in **Sahih Muslim**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "As for the people of Hell who will dwell therein, they will neither live nor die there."

There is a hard irony in the wording, and Ibn Kathir is the one who sets it up. He brings the scene from Sūrah al-Zukhruf where the people of the Fire call out to its keeper: "O Malik! Let your Lord make an end of us." He will say: "Verily, you shall abide forever." (43:77). The very thing they beg for — that an end be made of them — is the thing ayah 36 says will not happen. As Ibn Kathir explains: when they are in that state, they will think that if only they could die, it would be a time of rest for them, but that can never happen to them.

Notice what that tells us about their condition. Death, the thing every living creature flees, becomes the mercy they plead for and cannot get.

**"Nor shall its torment be lightened for them."** So the second escape route is closed too. If it will not end, might it at least ebb? Ibn Kathir gathers the ayat that answer: "Verily, the criminals will be in the torment of Hell to abide therein forever. (That) will not be lightened for them, and they will be plunged into destruction with deep regrets, sorrows and in despair therein." (43:74–75); "whenever it abates, We shall increase for them the fierceness of the Fire" (17:97); and "So taste you. No increase shall We give you, except in torment." (78:30).

Put together: no end, no easing, and no downward slope in intensity — the moment the Fire slackens it is fed again.

**"Thus do We requite every disbeliever."** Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase: "this is the recompense of everyone who disbelieved in his Lord and denied the truth." The ayah's own word for it is *requital* — not something arbitrary, but the matching answer to a life of denial.

## Ayah 37: the scream, and what they ask for

**"There they will be screaming."** The Arabic phrase is *wa hum yaṣṭarikhūna fīhā*, rendered in Ibn Kathir's text as "Therein they will cry" and in our translation as "There they will be ˹fervently˺ screaming." Ibn Kathir explains it simply: "they will call out in the Fire, beseeching Allah with their voices."

Take in what that means. In the Fire they are beseeching *Allah* — "**Our Lord!**" Compare that with the ayah Ibn Kathir cites a few lines later, describing how these same people lived: "when Allah Alone was invoked you disbelieved (denied), but when partners were joined to Him, you believed!" (40:12). The One they would not call on alone in this world is the only One they call on there. That recognition, arriving too late, is itself part of the punishment.

**What they ask is telling.** "Our Lord! Bring us out, we shall do righteous good deeds, not that we used to do." Ibn Kathir: "they will ask to go back to the worldly life so that they can do something different to the first deeds they did." So they are not asking for pardon without change; they are asking for time — another run at the life they wasted, with different actions this time.

**Why the plea is refused.** Ibn Kathir gives the reason with striking directness: "Allah, may He be glorified, knows that if He sent them back to this world, they would go back to what they had been forbidden to do, and He knows that they are lying, so He will not respond to their plea."

He supports this with the exchange in Sūrah Ghāfir, where they ask, "Then is there any way to get out (of the Fire)?" and are answered: "This is because, when Allah Alone was invoked you disbelieved (denied), but when partners were joined to Him, you believed!" (40:11–12). Ibn Kathir paraphrases the logic: there will be no response for you *because you were like that* — if you were returned to this world, you would just go back to what you had been forbidden.

This is not Allah refusing on a technicality. It is Allah judging by what a person actually is. Their promise in the Fire is sincere in the way a promise made under a knife is sincere: it expresses the pain, not the person.

## "Did We not give you a life long enough?"

Then comes the answer that turns the whole scene into an argument: **"Did We not give you lives long enough, so that whosoever would receive admonition could receive it? And the warner came to you."**

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: "did you not live for long enough in the world that if you were to be among those who would benefit from the truth, you would have benefited from it during your lifetimes?" Note the conditional built into the ayah — *so that whoever would take heed could take heed*. The lifetime was long enough for anyone willing to be reminded. The failure was not in the length of the opportunity but in the will to use it.

**From the Sunnah on the span of a life.** Ibn Kathir gathers several reports here, all from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him:

- **Imam Ahmad** recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has left no excuse for the person who lives to be sixty or seventy years old; Allah has left no excuse for him; Allah has left no excuse for him." (The threefold repetition is in the narration as Ibn Kathir gives it.)
- **Al-Bukhari**, in the Book of Riqaq in his *Sahih*: "Allah has left no excuse for a man who reaches the age of sixty."
- **Ibn Jarir** recorded: "Whoever is granted a long life until the age of sixty, Allah has left no excuse for him" — also recorded by **Imam Ahmad** and **An-Nasa'i** in Ar-Riqaq.
- And on why sixty is the benchmark: "The usual life span in my Ummah is between sixty and seventy years, and only a few pass this age" — recorded by **At-Tirmidhi** and **Ibn Majah** in the Book of Zuhd.

Ibn Kathir's point in stringing these together: sixty is the age at which Allah removes any excuse from His servants, and it is the usual age of people in this Ummah — so the ayah's "lives long enough" is not a hypothetical for a rare few. It is the ordinary human allowance.

**How much life is "enough"? The scholars differed on the benchmark.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the range of early opinions on what age the ayah has in view:

- Sayyidnā Ibn Husain Zain ul-ʿĀbidīn said: seventeen years.
- Qatādah said: eighteen years — meaning, in both cases, the age of puberty. Maʿārif notes the seventeen/eighteen difference is natural, since someone may reach puberty at seventeen and someone else at eighteen.
- Sayyidnā ʿAlī al-Murtaḍā said the age at which Allah has asked His sinning servants to beware is sixty.
- Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās is reported as forty years in one narration and sixty in another; Maʿārif notes that Ibn Kathir gave preference to the second.

**And it reconciles them rather than choosing.** In the Sharīʿah, Maʿārif explains, the age of puberty is the first line of demarcation: having crossed it, a person is blessed with enough reason to understand what is good or bad in his own case, which is why the precepts of the religion become binding from that point. So the address in ayah 37 is to disbelievers at large, whatever the length of their lives — someone who lived only a little past puberty was still given, by nature, enough power of discrimination to tell the true from the false, and deserves censure for not using it.

But sixty is such a long period of time that, in Maʿārif's reading, someone who had all those years, who saw all sorts of physical proofs scattered around him and heard the teachings of the prophets, and still did not recognise the truth — against him "the warning of Allah stood served ... in a more conclusive degree," and he is the more blameworthy. Both are guilty; the long-lived are more so. There is, as Maʿārif concludes, no contradiction between the narrations.

That is a sobering way to read a long life. We treat added years as a straightforward gift. The ayah treats them as evidence — and evidence cuts both ways depending on what was done with them.

## Who is "the warner"?

The second half of the argument is **"and the warner came to you"** (*wa jāʾakum al-nadhīr*). Two interpretations are reported.

**First: grey hair.** Ibn Kathir reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, ʿIkrimah, Abu Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, may Allah be pleased with him, Qatādah and Sufyān bin ʿUyaynah. Maʿārif puts the image beautifully: when the grey hairs flare up, they give a message to a person — *here comes the time to go.*

**Second: the Messenger ﷺ, and the messengers before him.** As-Suddī and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam held that it means the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Ibn Zayd recited "This is a warner of the (series of) warners of old" (53:56).

**Ibn Kathir's judgement.** He calls the second "the correct view," according to Shaybān, who narrated that Qatādah said: "Proof will be established against them by the fact that they lived long enough and that Messengers came to them." Ibn Jarīr favoured this too. Ibn Kathir adds that it is the apparent meaning of the ayah, and supports it from the Qur'an itself: the words that follow the keeper's reply, "Indeed We have brought the truth to you, but most of you have a hatred for the truth" (43:77–78), which he explains as *we showed you the truth clearly through the Messengers, but you rejected it and opposed it*; "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger" (17:15); and the exchange at the gates — "Every time a group is cast therein, its keepers will ask: 'Did no warner come to you?' They will say: 'Yes, indeed a warner did come to us, but we denied him...'" (67:8–9).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds both readings together: grey hair "might as well serve as the standard bearers of warning along with" the prophets and the scholars. And it broadens the point: all the conditions a person passes through after the age of puberty, and all minor and major changes in himself and his surroundings, are heralds of warning.

**What a *nadhīr* actually is.** Maʿārif pauses on the word, because "warner" in English sounds cold — it notes that the usual English renderings are makeshift, used for want of a suitable equivalent. A *nadhīr* is a person who, by virtue of his mercy and compassion, asks his people to stay away from things likely to bring them harm or total ruin, and tries to instil a fear of those things in their hearts so that they do not actually happen. In its well-recognised sense the word refers to the noble prophets, peace be upon them, and to the scholars who carry out their mission as their deputies.

Maʿārif then draws the two halves of ayah 37 together into one argument: from the age of puberty Allah gives a person enough ability to rationalise and to recognise at least his Creator and Master, and to live a life whose purpose is to seek His pleasure — human reason alone would have sufficed for that much. But Allah did not leave it simply at that. He also sent these special people, out of mercy, to help them reason it out and keep them safe from the false. So the case against the one who still refused rests on two pillars: an inner faculty, and an outward messenger.

**"So taste you. For the wrongdoers there is no helper."** Ibn Kathir: taste the punishment of the Fire as a recompense for going against the Prophets in all your deeds — "for today you will have no helper to save you from your fate of punishment and chains." In the world there was always someone to appeal to, some intercessor imagined, some protector assumed. On that Day there is no helper at all.

## Ayah 38: why the file is closed by His knowledge

**"Verily, Allah is the All-Knower of the Unseen of the heavens and the earth. Verily, He is the All-Knower of that which is in the breasts."**

Placed right after the refused plea, this is the ground of the whole verdict. Ibn Kathir: here Allah tells us that He knows the unseen in the heavens and earth, that He knows all that is hidden and the secrets of the hearts, and that He will reward or punish everyone according to his deeds.

Go back to ayah 37 with that in hand. The reason their promise — *bring us out and we will act differently* — receives no answer is stated in ayah 38: the One they are addressing knows what is in a chest. He is not weighing a claim He cannot verify.
