He knows the shape of the heart making it — which is exactly what Ibn Kathir said above: Allah knows that if He sent them back they would return to what they had been forbidden, and He knows that they are lying.

There is also a quiet comfort in the same attribute, and it belongs to the believer. If He knows all that is hidden and the secrets of the hearts, and rewards or punishes everyone according to his deeds, then the sincerity nobody witnessed is not lost, any more than hidden hypocrisy is missed.

## Living it

**Treat time as the thing being tested.** The plea in ayah 37 is a request for more time — the one commodity we currently hold and routinely waste. Whatever the person in the Fire would give to have back, we have now.

**Take the reminders as they come.** On Maʿārif's reading, the grey hair, the ageing body, the changing circumstance are all heralds of warning — sent in mercy, meant to be read, not resented.

**Answer the warner while he can still be answered.** Ayah 37 does not say the excuse ran out because the truth never arrived. It says the truth arrived and was refused. Every reminder heard and shelved is added to the record the ayah is describing.

**Fear a heart Allah knows better than you do.** Since ayah 38 tells us He knows what is in the breasts, the work is inward as much as outward: not merely doing what looks like obedience, but asking whether the intention behind it would survive being seen.

passages.title: Successors on earth and gods who created nothing
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat put two facts side by side and let the contrast do the work. The first is about us: we hold the earth as successors, each generation stepping into the place of the one before it (ayah 39). The second is about Allah: the false gods people call upon have created nothing and own nothing, while the heavens and the earth themselves stay in place only because Allah holds them (ayat 40–41). What binds the passage together is a single question — who actually has the power here? — and the commentators trace the answer through both halves.

## Where the passage begins: nothing is hidden

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 39 as flowing directly out of the ayah before it. There Allah has just told us that He is the All-Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and the All-Knower of what is in the breasts. Ibn Kathir draws out the point: Allah knows all that is hidden and the secrets of the hearts, and He will reward or punish everyone according to his deeds.

That is the platform on which ayah 39 stands. Before we are told that we are successors on earth, we are told that the One who handed the earth over knows exactly what we do with it — including the part of us no one else ever sees.

## Ayah 39: "successors on earth"

**The word itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key term: *khalāʾif* (خَلَائِف) is the plural of *khalīfah* (خَلِيفَة), which means deputy or vice-regent. The plural matters. Allah does not say He made you *a* deputy; He made you deputies, a succession of them.

Ibn Kathir gives the same sense in the plainest possible terms: **all people succeed one another, generation after generation.** He points to a parallel elsewhere in the Qurʼān, "and makes you inheritors of the earth, generations after generations" (27:62), so that the picture is of an inheritance passing hand to hand rather than a possession settled on anyone.

**What that is meant to do to you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point into something you can feel. Allah has let human beings have lands and houses that keep passing on from one owner to the next — and, it says, *in this phenomenon there is a great lesson: turn to Allah.*

*(A reflection of my own, not the commentators': think of any house or field you know. Someone else stood where you stand now, and someone else will stand there after you. The paperwork with your name on it records a handover, not an ownership that stops with you.)*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then offers a second, complementary reading of the address: the words may be spoken to the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ — *after past communities, We made you take their place, with authority to make life better around you.* On that reading the ayah carries a duty in two directions. Backwards: learn your lesson from what happened to the peoples who held this place before you. Forwards: since you have been given authority to make life better around you, do not, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, while away the precious moments of your life in negligence.

So *khalīfah* here is not a compliment about human grandeur. It is a station held on the way to a handover.

**"So whoever disbelieves — upon him is his disbelief."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and closes off every escape route: *he and no one else will have to bear the consequences of that.* Nobody carries it for you. What passes down the generations, on the picture the ayah has just drawn, is property; the consequence of disbelief stays with the one who chose it.

**Disbelief only ever adds.** The ayah then says something striking twice over: the disbelief of the disbelievers adds nothing but *maqt* — hatred — in the sight of their Lord; and it adds them nothing but loss.

Ibn Kathir explains it as a matter of accumulation over time: *the longer they persist in their disbelief, the more Allah hates them, and the longer they persist in it, the more they and their families will lose on the Day of Resurrection.* Note what this corrects. A long life is easily counted as gain — more years, more property, more standing. On Ibn Kathir's reading the ledger runs the other way: what is actually accumulating is hatred in the sight of the Lord, and loss. Every added year of turning away adds to the total.

**The mirror image.** Ibn Kathir does not leave the believer out of the equation. He sets the opposite case directly against it: *this is in contrast to the believers, for the longer they live and do good deeds, the higher their status in Paradise will be, the greater their reward, and the more beloved they will be to their Creator.* The same passage of time, the same accumulating principle — running in the opposite direction.

## Ayah 40: four questions and no answer

Now the address turns. Allah instructs His Messenger ﷺ, as Ibn Kathir puts it, to say to the idolaters — and what follows is not an argument so much as a cross-examination. Ibn Kathir titles this section *The Helplessness of the false gods and the Power of Allah.*

**"Have you considered your partners whom you call upon besides Allah?"** Ibn Kathir identifies who is meant: *the idols and rivals.* Notice the possessive — *your* partners. They are the ones the idolaters themselves call upon. The claim is being handed back to its authors for inspection.

**"Show Me what they have created of the earth."** *Arūnī* — show me. It is a challenge with no exit: not "argue for it", but "point to it". Name one thing on this earth your gods brought into being. Ibn Kathir's answer is total: *they have nothing at all of that* — and he adds a deliberately tiny image: *they do not possess even the membrane covering the stone of a date.* That thin skin around a date stone is the entire estate of every false god ever worshipped.

**"Or have they any share in the heavens?"** Having been shut out of the earth, the claim is chased upward — perhaps a partnership, some junior share in the heavens? Ibn Kathir folds this into the same verdict: they have nothing at all of that either. Both floors of creation are searched and the idols hold no title on either.

**"Or have We given them a Book, so that they act on clear proof therefrom?"** This is the last door. If there is no evidence in creation, is there evidence in revelation? Ibn Kathir puts the question in the idolaters' own mouths — *have We revealed to them a Book on which they base their shirk and disbelief?* — and answers: *this is not the case at all.*

Take the shape of the whole ayah in. Every ground the idolaters might have offered for worshipping something besides Allah has now been named and eliminated: what their gods created in the earth, what share they hold in the heavens, what Book was revealed to them to act on. Nothing is left standing.

**"Nay, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion."** So what is holding their religion up, if not evidence? Ibn Kathir answers: *they are merely following their own whims, opinions and wishes which are their personal desires, and they are no more than misguidance and falsehood.*

The word the ayah uses is *ghurūr*, rendered here as delusion. And notice that they promise it *to one another*. That is the mechanism laid bare: with no created thing to point to, no share in the heavens, and no Book, what remains is a circle of people reassuring each other. It has the look of consensus; Ibn Kathir's verdict on what is actually underneath it is whim, opinion and personal desire — misguidance and falsehood.

## Ayah 41: the hand that holds the heavens

Then, says Ibn Kathir, Allah tells us of His mighty power — the power by which the heavens and the earth stand by His command, and the forces He has placed between them to hold them.

**"Indeed Allah grasps the heavens and the earth lest they should move away from their places."** Ibn Kathir's gloss: *lest they should shift from where they are.* He gathers two parallels from elsewhere in the Qurʼān: "He withholds the heaven from falling on the earth except by His leave" (22:65), and "And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command" (30:25).

This is the answer to ayah 40 delivered as a fact rather than a rebuttal. The idols do not possess so much as the membrane on a date stone; Allah grasps the heavens and the earth. The two are not in the same category and never were.

**A careful note on what this does *not* say.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise caution, because readers reach for cosmology here. The 'holding' of the heavens does not mean that their movement was stopped. It means holding them from moving *askance* — and the wording bears this out: *an tazūlā* (أَن تَزُولَا) means *from leaving their existing state.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore concludes that in this ayah there is no supporting evidence on either side as to whether the skies move or are static.

**"And if they were to move away from their places, there is not one that could grasp them after Him."** Ibn Kathir: *no one can make them stay and preserve them except Him.* There is no second holder, no reserve arrangement.

**"Truly He is Ever Most Forbearing, Oft-Forgiving."** And now the turn. After naming His grasp on the heavens and the earth, the ayah closes with *Ḥalīm* and *Ghafūr* — Ever Most Forbearing and Oft-Forgiving.

Ibn Kathir explains exactly why these two names belong here: *He is Ever Most Forbearing and Oft-Forgiving because He sees His servants disbelieving in Him and disobeying Him, yet He is patient and gives them time, He waits and does not hasten the punishment, and He conceals the faults of others and forgives them.*

Put the two halves of the ayah together and the effect is overwhelming. The One who grasps the heavens and the earth so that they do not shift is the same One being disbelieved in by the people standing beneath them — and on Ibn Kathir's reading He is patient, gives them time, and does not hasten the punishment. *Ḥalīm* here means seeing it, being able, and waiting. *Ghafūr* is the further step Ibn Kathir names: not merely delay, but concealing faults and forgiving them.

## Living it

*The four points below are my own application of what the two commentaries say — the sourced explanation is above.*

**Hold your place on earth with an open hand.** Ayah 39 tells you what you are: a *khalīfah*, a deputy standing in a place that keeps passing from one holder to the next. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names both duties this creates — take the lesson from those who stood here before you, and use the authority you have been given to make life better around you rather than letting your days slip past in negligence. And it names the response the whole phenomenon is meant to produce: turn to Allah.

**Read your own life as an accumulating total.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 39 cuts both ways. If a long life of persisting in disbelief only adds hatred in the sight of the Lord and loss, then a long life of faith and good deeds only adds rank in Paradise, reward, and belovedness to your Creator. Today is not neutral; it is being added to one side or the other.

**Audit what you rely on.** Ayah 40 puts its questions to the idolaters, and they are worth turning on ourselves: does this conviction rest on anything real, or does it stand only because the people around me keep affirming it to each other? Ibn Kathir's diagnosis of the latter is worth remembering — whims, opinions and personal desires — and the ayah's own word for what such people promise one another is *ghurūr*, delusion.

**Let ayah 41 correct how you read Allah's patience.** When you see wrongdoing continue and nothing appears to happen, Ibn Kathir tells you what is really the case: He sees His servants disbelieving and disobeying, and He is patient, gives them time, and does not hasten the punishment. That should stop you from despairing at delay. It should also stop you from mistaking the delay for permission, since ayah 39 has already said what persisting in disbelief is quietly adding up to. And in the same breath it is an open door, because the ayah does not end at forbearance. It ends at forgiveness.

passages.title: Broken oaths, arrogant plotting, and delayed punishment
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Sūrah Fāṭir with a case brought against the Quraysh and the Arabs who rejected the Messenger ﷺ: they had once sworn the most binding oath that if only a warner were sent to them they would out-do every nation in guidance — and when the warner actually came, they ran. What holds the passage together is the movement from that broken oath (ayah 42) to what lay underneath it — arrogance and scheming (ayah 43) — then to the fate of every earlier people who did the same (ayah 44), and finally to the mercy that explains why the sky has not yet fallen on those doing it now (ayah 45).

## The oath they made before he came

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us here how the Quraysh and the Arabs swore by Allah their most binding oath **before** the Messenger ﷺ came to them. The Arabic is وَأَقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أَيْمَانِهِمْ — rendered by Ibn Kathir as their "most binding oath," and in the translation as their "most solemn oaths." Not a casual promise, then, but the strongest form of undertaking they knew, sworn in the name of Allah Himself.

And the claim was extravagant: لَيَكُونُنَّ أَهْدَىٰ مِنْ إِحْدَى الْأُمَمِ — "they would be more guided than any of the nations." Ibn Kathir notes, citing Ad-Dahhak and others, that the nations meant are those to whom Messengers had already been sent — the communities of the earlier Books. In other words: *look at how those people treated their prophets; if a prophet came to us, we would do better than all of them.*

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two other passages where the Qur'an records the same self-confident boast. In Sūrat al-Anʿām, Allah warns them against saying, "The Book was sent down only to two sects before us, and for our part, we were in fact unaware of what they studied," or, "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than they" — and then answers them: "So, now has come unto you a clear proof from your Lord, and a guidance and a mercy. Who then does more wrong than one who rejects the Ayat of Allah and turns away therefrom?" (6:156–157). And in Sūrat aṣ-Ṣāffāt: "And indeed they used to say: 'If we had a reminder as had the men of old, We would have indeed been the chosen servants of Allah!' But they disbelieve therein, so they will come to know!" (37:167–170).

The three passages read together make one point with unmistakable force. The excuse was pre-emptively demolished. They had told Allah exactly what they would do if He sent them a warner. He sent them one. Then they did the opposite.

## "It increased in them nothing but flight"

فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ نَذِيرٌ — "yet when a warner came to them." Ibn Kathir identifies the warner precisely: Muhammad ﷺ, with the Book revealed to him, the Clear Qur'an. This is what they had asked for, and more than they had asked for.

The response is given in one devastating word: مَا زَادَهُمْ إِلَّا نُفُورًا — "it increased in them nothing but flight (from the truth)." Ibn Kathir's gloss is that "they only increased in their disbelief." Notice the shape of the sentence: the coming of the warner did not leave them where they were. Revelation is never neutral. What was meant to guide them became, through their own response to it, an accelerant of what was already in their hearts — the very opposite of what they had sworn on oath.

It is worth sitting with the honesty of this. They did not fail for lack of evidence, nor for lack of desire — they had actively wished for a warner. The failure came after the wish was granted.

## What the flight was really made of: arrogance and plotting

Ayah 43 opens by naming the two things that produced that flight. Ibn Kathir reads اسْتِكْبَارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ, "arrogance in the land," as the reason they took flight: **they were too arrogant to follow the signs of Allah.** Not unconvinced — too proud. The signs were there; submitting to them meant coming down from a height they were unwilling to leave.

And وَمَكْرَ السَّيِّئِ, "the plotting of evil," Ibn Kathir explains as this: **they plotted to prevent people from following the path of Allah.** Arrogance turned outward becomes obstruction. It is not enough to refuse the road oneself; the proud man wants the road closed.

These two — inner haughtiness and outward scheming — are the anatomy of rejection as this passage draws it. And the very next clause tells us where such scheming ends up.

## "The evil plot encompasses only him who makes it"

وَلَا يَحِيقُ الْمَكْرُ السَّيِّئُ إِلَّا بِأَهْلِهِ. Ibn Kathir: "the evil consequences of that will come back upon them and not on others."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key verb. *Lā yaḥīq* carries the sense of *lā yuḥīṭ* (does not surround) or *lā yuṣīb* (does not afflict). The image is of a plot as something that **encircles** — and the ring closes on the one who drew it. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: the curse of making an evil plan falls on none but the one who makes it; a person who wishes evil for others himself falls victim to it.

### The obvious objection — and two answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not let this pass without raising the doubt any honest reader feels. In everyday life we constantly see a schemer get away with it, while the harm he intended lands squarely on his innocent target. How can it be said that the plot afflicts nobody but its author?

**The first answer**, from Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi (raḥimahu'Llāh): the pain or loss inflicted on the victim was a loss limited to this mortal world, whereas the loss awaiting the maker of the plan in the Hereafter is both heavier and more lasting. Set the two side by side and the schemer's apparent worldly gain amounts to nothing. The ayah is not denying that innocent people suffer; it is telling you where the real, final weight of the transaction falls.

**The second answer**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from some of the elders: there are in fact many occasions when the curse of contriving against an innocent person, or of inflicting injustice on him, falls on its author right here in this world as well. Muhammad Ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said that there are three things whose doer does not remain safe against their curse and punishment even in this world:

1. Causing harm or pain to some innocent person by engineering evil against him,
2. Inflicting any injustice,
3. Breaking of pledge.

(Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Ibn Kathir.) And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is particularly so when such things are done against a person who is helpless, or who does not have the power to avenge himself, or who chooses to endure despite having that power. Experience, it says, bears out that no one who does things like that has ever remained unaffected by the curse of the injustice he inflicted, even in this world.

Look at that list of three again next to ayah 42. **Breaking of pledge** is precisely what the Quraysh had done: they swore by Allah, and then broke the oath. So the general rule stated in ayah 43 is not an abstraction dropped into the middle of the passage — it lands directly on the men described in ayah 42.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the discussion with a careful piece of scholarly restraint. The *ḥaṣr* — the restriction implied by "none but its own people" — appears here in terms of a majority rule rather than in any absolute sense. And it ends, as the scholars do: **Allah knows best.**

## Allah's Sunnah does not change

فَهَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَّا سُنَّتَ الْأَوَّلِينَ — "Then, can they expect anything else but the Sunnah of the peoples of old?" The word *Sunnah* is glossed here as Allah's way of dealing with people. Ibn Kathir specifies what that way was: **the punishment of Allah for disbelieving in His Messengers and going against His command.**

Then two words seal it off. فَلَنْ تَجِدَ لِسُنَّتِ اللَّهِ تَبْدِيلًا — no *tabdīl*: Ibn Kathir says it does not change or alter, and this is what happens to every disbeliever. وَلَنْ تَجِدَ لِسُنَّتِ اللَّهِ تَحْوِيلًا — no *taḥwīl*, which Ibn Kathir explains with another ayah: "But when Allah wills a people's punishment, there can be no turning back of it" (13:11) — meaning, as he says, no one can remove that from them or ward it off from them.

Read with those two glosses, the two words are doing different work, and that is why both are there. The law itself does not change or alter — you cannot have it replaced with a more comfortable one. And once the punishment is willed, it cannot be turned back — no one can lift it off you or fend it away. There is no negotiating with the law and no dodging it. Ibn Kathir closes the point where a scholar should: **and Allah knows best.**

## "Have they not travelled through the land?"

Ayah 44 turns the argument from law to evidence. Ibn Kathir renders the address as a command to the Prophet ﷺ: *say, O Muhammad, to these people who disbelieve the Message you have brought:* travel in the land and see what the punishment of those who disbelieved the Messengers actually was — how Allah destroyed them completely; and a similar end awaits the disbelievers.

Then he makes the reader look at the ruins in detail: **see how their homes were emptied of them**, and how they lost everything after living in luxury, being so numerous, so well equipped, and having so much wealth and so many children. The ayah itself says those earlier peoples "were superior to them in power." All of it, Ibn Kathir says, was of no avail to them and could not protect them in the slightest from the punishment of Allah when the command of the Lord came.

This is a Qur'anic method worth naming: the argument is not made by assertion but by asking people to go and look. Dead cities are the exhibit. Arrogance in the land (ayah 43) is answered by a walk through the land (ayah 44).

Then: "Allah is not such that anything in the heavens or in the earth escapes Him." Nothing is impossible for Him, Ibn Kathir says, when He wants it to happen in the heavens or on the earth. And the closing names — إِنَّهُ كَانَ عَلِيمًا قَدِيرًا, "Verily, He is All-Knowing, All-Able" — he glosses simply: **He knows all that exists and is able to do all things.** Knowledge locates; power executes. Held together, they close every escape route the schemer of ayah 43 imagines he has.

## The mercy of the delay

If Allah is All-Knowing and All-Able, and His Sunnah with deniers never changes, the honest question is: why is anyone still standing? Ayah 45 answers it, and Ibn Kathir titles the answer *the wisdom behind delaying the punishment*.

وَلَوْ يُؤَاخِذُ اللَّهُ النَّاسَ بِمَا كَسَبُوا مَا تَرَكَ عَلَىٰ ظَهْرِهَا مِنْ دَابَّةٍ — "And if Allah were to punish men for that which they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth." Ibn Kathir: if He were to punish them for all of their sins, He would destroy all the people of the earth and all that they own of livestock and crops.

Notice how far the ruin would reach. Not "He would not leave a man," but **not a moving creature** — *dābbah* — and Ibn Kathir extends it to their livestock and their crops. Sin is charged to human beings, yet the consequence would sweep the animals away with them. Saʿīd bin Jubayr and As-Suddī explained the mechanism: it means He would have stopped sending rain to them, and all the animals would have died as a result. That is a startling picture of how tightly our moral life and the world around us are bound together: the punishment arrives as a withheld rain-cloud, and the animals starve.

وَلَٰكِن يُؤَخِّرُهُمْ إِلَىٰ أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى — "but He gives them respite to an appointed term." Ibn Kathir explains: He is delaying until the Day of Resurrection, when He will bring them to account and reward or punish each one according to his deeds — rewarding those who obeyed Him and punishing those who disobeyed Him.

So the delay is not indifference and it is not weakness; it is a *named*, fixed appointment. Every day the sun rises on a world full of sin is a day of respite, not of acquittal.

And the passage — with it, the whole sūrah — ends on a gaze rather than a blow: فَإِذَا جَاءَ أَجَلُهُمْ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ بِعِبَادِهِ بَصِيرًا, "and when their term comes, then verily, Allah is Ever All-Seer of His servants." He calls them *His servants* even here, and He is *Baṣīr*, ever-seeing them. Nothing done in the dark of a plot was unobserved; nothing endured by the wronged went unwitnessed.

## Living it

**Beware of the promise made in need.** They swore an oath while the warner was still only a wish. When the wish was granted, the oath collapsed. All of us bargain like this — *if I get through this, I will change* — and ayah 42 is a mirror held up to exactly that. Watch what you do after the answer arrives, not what you say before it.

**Guidance can harden as easily as soften.** That a warner's coming "increased in them nothing but flight" should keep any of us from assuming that mere exposure to the Qur'an is safety. What we do with it decides which way it moves us.

**Take the warning about scheming personally.** Read al-Qurazī's three — harming an innocent by engineering evil against him, inflicting injustice, breaking a pledge — as the list they are, and note the special warning about mistreating someone helpless, or someone who forbears when they could retaliate. The ring you draw closes on you.

**And read the delay as the invitation it is.** You are still here, rain is still falling, the appointed term has not come. That is the gap ayah 45 opens up — and it exists so that a servant can turn back before it closes.
